_Why does an admitted plan still need permission on every control tick?_

A trajectory can be feasible when it arrives and become unsafe while the machine follows it. The body lags its reference, a payload or a hot motor erodes braking authority, a person steps into the path, or the learned proposer stalls with its last command still in force. A machine that checks only before motion begins discovers these changes after the energy is already moving, and the proposer cannot be trusted to notice them, because nothing in its output bounds stopping distance, actuator effort, or timing. Learned proposals therefore need an independent permission path that re-checks current conditions on every tick, keeps useful motion inside a stopping envelope, corrects a command when a feasible correction exists, and holds a response it can execute without the proposer before the remaining margin is spent. Each of those guarantees depends on bounded sensing error, available actuator force, and a decision delivered on time. Enforcement joins these conditions at the causal boundary, where a permitted command becomes motion that software cannot undo.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate the finished stopping budget and its speed ceiling, treating the tracking bound as a premise the enforcer monitors on every tick
- Derive how momentum and commanded effort change the remaining safety margin, and the contact force at a latch and at a handover that caps approach speed
- Explain how a control barrier function limits motion while its model, sensing, actuator, and timing assumptions hold
- Formulate a quadratic program that minimally adjusts a proposal within feasible actuator and safety constraints
- Select state-matched fallback responses when sensing, computation, or actuator limits invalidate normal enforcement
- Distinguish the permission path's unrated performance checks from the certified drive, scanner, and arm safety functions that carry the protective claim beneath it
- Construct an enforcement record and formulate the admitted command that binds each check to its detector, its fallback response, and the records it consumes

:::

## The Per-Tick Gatekeeper {#sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper}

Every physical AI system ends in the same act. A command leaves software, becomes current in a motor winding, and puts momentum into a world that does not roll back. Safety enforcement is the runtime mechanism that decides, one control tick at a time, whether the next command may cross that causal boundary. Checking a plan once before it runs does not settle the question, because admission judges the plan against the state the planner predicted, and the machine then executes it against the state it actually reaches. Between those two moments the body can lag its reference, an actuator can run short of torque, a person can step into the aisle, and the learned proposer can stall or emit a setpoint the plan never contained. Enforcement exists so that none of these events is discovered only after the energy has been delivered.

The central constraint is that the learned proposer can neither be trusted with that decision nor be discarded. Its competence is what makes the machine useful, yet nothing in its output bounds stopping distance, actuator effort, or timing. Enforcement resolves the tension by separating proposal from permission, the third law (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}), and by giving the permission side three jobs. It must hold a stopping reservation, the clearance the machine needs to arrest its motion from the current state; it must correct a proposal minimally when a feasible correction exists; and it must select a response it can execute without the proposer when none does. The chapter builds the three jobs in that order.

On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the safety microcontroller (MCU) admits the run down the aisle only after the matched stop suffix named in its trajectory record is resident in the MCU's memory and feasible from the commitment entry state defined in @sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines. Commitment is the instant after which the machine can no longer abandon the plan's motion without that latched suffix, so the suffix is matched to the state the machine will have at that instant, not to the states it passes through on the way. Before commitment, a different response must cover the motion. Admission requires an independently executable, state-matched fallback from every state reachable up to that instant. It also requires a bounded representation of the S-curve suffix that the MCU can decode, validate, and execute within its declared workload (the polynomial layout of @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory is an illustrative encoding rather than that S-curve representation). Because that admission step checks the plan only once before motion starts, the machine still executes the plan one millisecond tick at a time, and enforcement is the check made on every one of those ticks together with the response it selects when even the resident stop no longer fits.

The rest of the chapter follows the running machine through that per-tick check. The starting point is the deficit planning left open, when the jerk-limited stop carried the base's stopping budget past the rack-end clearance at the drive limit while the body's departure from its reference remained unpriced. Once the tracking bound supplies that missing spatial term, the finished stopping budget fixes the reservation and a candidate aisle speed that still requires physical qualification. Actuator saturation then reveals how quickly that reservation shrinks once gravity or thermal limits spend braking authority. A control barrier function turns the reservation into a constraint on the next command. A least-change filter can then correct a violating proposal, both in free space and in contact, inside a declared cycle budget on a processor the proposer cannot preempt. When a check fails or a lease expires, the fallback hierarchy supplies the surviving hardware response, and the chapter closes with the infrastructure failures that break these premises and the enforcement record that binds every check to its evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The trajectory record and the matched stop suffix it names are established in @sec-planning-trajectory-contract.
:::

An invalid command must be intercepted before it reaches the drive, because once current in a winding imparts momentum, an exception handler cannot recall it. Enforcement therefore keeps the task competence of learned policies while denying them authority over geometric clearance, thermal limits, and human-safety invariants. The enforcer\index{Enforcer}, the permission path's per-tick gatekeeper, sits on the permission side of the proposal boundary. It is a hard real-time component that evaluates candidate proposals, verifies invariant state bounds, and holds the exclusive hardware authority to permit current flow or command a fallback stop.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The per-tick permission cadence on which the enforcer runs is established in @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_pa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan-to-Act gating edge."}
*Enforcement sits on the Plan-to-Act edge: no proposal reaches a drive unchecked.*
:::

In the architecture this chapter follows, the enforcer executes on a dedicated microcontroller wired to the sensing and drive interfaces it needs. It checks each candidate command before the drive can apply it. A packet firewall offers a limited software analogy: a sender may request an operation without having authority to perform it. Unlike a packet filter, the enforcer must also account for momentum already present in the plant and preserve an achievable response when it refuses a request.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The silicon placement that keeps the permission path independent of the proposer is developed in @sec-placement-isolation-decisions.
:::

The architecture separates a capable proposer, a resident protective controller, and an output selector. This is the **Simplex architecture**\index{Simplex architecture!dual-controller model}[^fn-simplex-online-upgrade] [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using], the runtime-assurance pattern that @sec-boundary-machine-model first named. The proposer supplies useful candidates, while the permission path retains the exclusive ability to select a physically feasible response without waiting for it. The first quantity the enforcer needs is how far the body can stray from the reference it is asked to follow, because every clearance the permission path defends must also contain that error.

[^fn-simplex-online-upgrade]: **Simplex Architecture**: The design came from Carnegie Mellon in the 1990s as a way to upgrade the controller of a running plant without stopping it. An untested new controller drove the plant while a simple verified controller and a switching rule stood ready to take it back [@seto1998simplex]. The learned proposer occupies the untested controller's seat, and the design's premise, that the region from which the verified controller can still recover is known in advance, is the stopping envelope this chapter computes. \index{Simplex architecture!online upgrade}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-lease-stop
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TIMING CONTRACT AND THE LEASE-EXPIRY WORST CASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the lease paragraph below; the cycle timeline, @tbl-12-fallback-hierarchy,
# │          the enforcement record, and the summary reuse these strings.
# │ Goal:    state the three timers and the delay from last renewal to brake onset.
# │ Show:    chunk rate, lease, heartbeat rate and timeout, self-watchdog,
# │          tick, bus cycle, brake onset, renewal-to-onset delay; the
# │          evidence-age refusal threshold (budgeted observation age plus the
# │          clock-conversion bound) read by cycle stage 2 and the record. The
# │          base stall is priced in calc-enforcement-stopping-budget, after the
# │          spare is set.
# │ How:     the same RM/AISLE fields that size the lease in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementLeaseStop:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    heartbeat_rate = AISLE.heartbeat_rate  # category: chosen
    heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (observation age the budget charges, row 5)
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    renewal_to_onset = (lease + tick + bus + onset).to(millisecond)
    age_threshold = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # dispatch-age qualification threshold

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunk_period < lease, "One chunk period must fit inside the lease.")
    check(heartbeat_timeout < lease, "A total host stall must trip the heartbeat before the lease expires.")
    check(abs(lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "The chunk lease is 60 ms.")
    check(abs(renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Brake onset comes 82 ms after the last valid renewal.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, "The budgeted observation age is 51.6 ms.")
    check(abs(age_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, "The dispatch-age qualification threshold is 51.8 ms.")
    # fig12_canonical_fallback_ladder.svg and parts/images/svg/fig_part3_record_chain.svg draw 1 kHz, 60 ms, and 51.6 ms from these guards.
    check(abs(tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "The hand-drawn figures label the MCU tick 1 kHz.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate_hz_str = fmt(chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    lease_ms_str = fmt_latency(lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    heartbeat_rate_hz_str = fmt(heartbeat_rate.to(hertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    heartbeat_timeout_ms_str = fmt_latency(heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    self_watchdog_ms_str = fmt_latency(self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tick_ms_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tick_us_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    loop_rate_str = fmt_frequency((1 / tick).to(hertz))
    bus_ms_str = fmt_latency(bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    onset_ms_str = fmt_latency(onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_to_onset_ms_str = fmt_latency(renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_threshold_str = fmt_latency(age_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

## The Tracker Handoff and Dynamic Reference Envelopes {#sec-enforcement-handoff}

Even when communication latency is zero and the permission path admits every reference command without delay, physical robots follow reference trajectories imperfectly. Mechanical compliance, inertia, and non-ideal motor dynamics produce tracking discrepancies. The feedback tracker, the closed-loop controller that turns admitted references into actuator effort, must bound this deviation across the entire maneuver. The bound is a **worst-case tracking error tube** ($\TrackingErrorBound$), an upper bound on the spatial departure of the tracked position output from its nominal reference. For Cartesian point tracking, $\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant)$ and $\ReferencePosition(\TimeInstant)$ denote the actual and reference positions evaluated in the same spatial frame. For whole-body systems such as mobile manipulators, the execution stack defines a declared output map or metric weighting that bounds the maximum physical swept-volume displacement in meters. The safety enforcer depends directly on this bound. Any spatial clearance reserved around a planned reference path must guarantee physical containment of the actual robot body.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The admitted setpoints and feedforward torques that the tracker turns into actuator effort are established in @sec-planning-handoff.
:::

Provided that the physical system begins within an initial qualified error region and its operating parameters (reference velocity, command acceleration, payload mass, external disturbances, and actuator temperature) stay within their validated operating envelope, the feedback controller guarantees the transient position-error bound:
$$\|\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant) - \ReferencePosition(\TimeInstant)\| \le \TrackingErrorBound \quad \forall \TimeInstant \ge 0.$$
This guarantee forms a software contract between the tracking layer and the safety enforcer\index{Enforcer!tracking contract}. Rather than re-analyzing raw plant dynamics or reconstructing low-level controller state on every millisecond control cycle, the enforcer consumes this certified error bound as an invariant. However, this contract confines physical motion to the $\TrackingErrorBound$\index{Tracking error bound} tube only while the operational conditions used to establish the certificate remain valid.

The magnitude of $\TrackingErrorBound$ is a physical distance dictated by hardware properties: reflected rotor inertia ($\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$), gearbox backlash, structural compliance, and actuator torque saturation\index{Actuator torque limits}. While a steady-state stiffness calculation balances constant external disturbances against closed-loop restoring force\index{Closed-loop stiffness}, steady-state metrics fail to capture transient overshoot, phase lag, or settling oscillations excited during aggressive maneuvers. Consequently, engineering teams cannot rely on static linear approximations; they must support the tracking tube bound $\TrackingErrorBound$ with a bounded plant and controller model, defined operating limits, and full-envelope dynamic qualification tests. Tests can expose an invalid bound; the tested trajectories alone do not prove containment for every admissible maneuver.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reflected rotor inertia, $\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$, is established in @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-tracking-bound
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE BASE'S TRACKING BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the tracking-bound paragraphs immediately below.
# │ Goal:    state the inset the enforcer applies and what a doubled error costs.
# │ Show:    the base's tracking bound and the error if wear doubled it.
# │ How:     AISLE.eps_track, the same field row 7 of the stopping budget uses.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementTrackingBound:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_doubled = (2 * eps_track).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "The base's tracking bound is 40 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_doubled_str = fmt_length(eps_doubled, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

For the baseline warehouse mobile manipulator, the illustrative dynamic qualification target is $\TrackingErrorBound =$ `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide). The tracking controller sustains this bound only while three coupled operational constraints remain satisfied. First, reference trajectories must not demand accelerations exceeding drive torque limits. Second, external disturbance forces must remain below $\DisturbanceForceBound$, the qualified bound on external disturbance force. Last, actuator coils must operate below their continuous thermal derating thresholds\index{Joule heating} and DC bus voltage limits. A reference trajectory demanding acceleration beyond peak torque drives the actuators into saturation\index{Actuator saturation}, causing the physical chassis to lag behind the command. Without aggressive anti-windup clamping, the integrator state accumulates severe windup\index{Integrator windup}, prolonging recovery long after the reference demand subsides. Outside this qualified operating envelope, the tracking certificate is void, and the system loses its guaranteed error bound.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Continuous thermal derating of motor windings is established in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
:::

Because the physical robot can deviate from its planned reference by up to $\TrackingErrorBound$ in any direction, the safety architecture must subtract this uncertainty margin directly from the admissible workspace. Let $\BarrierFunction$ measure the spatial clearance remaining around a reference. To guarantee that the physical robot maintains non-negative clearance, the enforcer applies an inset contraction:
$$\ContractedBarrierFunction(\ReferencePosition) = \BarrierFunction(\ReferencePosition) - \TrackingErrorBound \ge 0.$$
A reference trajectory that maintains nominal clearance $\NominalReferenceClearance$ from a warehouse rack upright guarantees the physical chassis only $\NominalReferenceClearance - \TrackingErrorBound$ of actual clearance. Consequently, the safety enforcer evaluates reference commands against a contracted boundary that adds `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` to the nominal buffer. As detailed in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes, this tracking inset compounds directly with stopping distance budgets, where localization uncertainty and transport delay consume additional clearance. Mechanical wear poses an insidious operational risk here. If worn drive bearings, tire degradation, or altered motor parameters double the true tracking error to `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_doubled_str` without updating the enforcer's parameter registry, the physical base consumes an unbudgeted `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` of clearance that the enforcer assumes remains available. An unmodeled tracking degradation silently undermines every higher-level safety margin.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Clearance insets that absorb spatial sensing error are established in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
:::

To maintain safety guarantees in production, the runtime monitoring stack must treat $\TrackingErrorBound$ as an actively verified contract rather than a static design assumption. The underlying real-time middleware publishes $\TrackingErrorBound$ alongside its validity envelope, while hardware monitors estimate the instantaneous tracking error $\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant) = \|\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant) - \ReferencePosition(\TimeInstant)\|$ on every `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` controller tick. Agreement with encoder-reported position is a runtime proxy, not independent evidence of physical localization; the localization allowance must contain drift that these channels cannot expose. If an observable disturbance or actuator thermal throttling causes the monitored $\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)$ to exceed $\TrackingErrorBound$, the tracking contract is broken. Upon detecting this violation, the safety enforcer revokes the admitted command and activates a state-matched emergency fallback maneuver. Maintaining physical containment during this transition requires that the fallback braking trajectory remains dynamically feasible even after the tracking bound is lost.

::: {#psp-enforcement-inset-margin .callout-perspective title="The inset margin invariant"}
A spatial stopping boundary must reserve margin for the tracking loop's qualified error bound. The runtime stopping envelope (@eq-enforce-stopping-envelope) incorporates this geometric inset alongside displacement accumulated during transport lag\index{Transport lag} before admitting reference trajectories. When the safety barrier certificates\index{Barrier certificates} of @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission are formulated in non-spatial coordinates (such as energy or momentum limits), the safety layer must map the tracking tube into a corresponding conservative bound on barrier variation, rather than subtracting a scalar distance. Evaluating barrier certificates against nominal trajectory geometry alone risks admitting references whose physical tracking tubes intersect obstacle boundaries.
:::

Control theory provides rich methodologies for synthesizing tracking controllers, state observers, and disturbance rejection algorithms [@slotine1991applied; @astrom2021feedback]. In embedded industrial robotics, systems frequently deploy a **cascaded control hierarchy**\index{Cascaded control!tracking architecture}, where outer position loops feed intermediate velocity setpoints down to high-rate current loops. Alternatively, a **tracking Model Predictive Controller (MPC)**\index{Model Predictive Control!tracking layer} solves an online optimization problem over a receding horizon to generate optimal corrective control actions while respecting actuator bounds. From the perspective of the safety enforcer, the specific internal architecture of the tracking controller is abstracted away; the safety filter requires only that the chosen implementation certifies and guarantees a concrete tracking bound $\TrackingErrorBound$ under specified operational conditions.

A tracking controller may establish convergence to the reference path under its qualified model and operating conditions. That result supplies no collision-avoidance guarantee. A well-tuned tracker will follow an erroneous trajectory directly into a warehouse support column with high precision. Control Lyapunov functions[^fn-clf-tracking-convergence] mathematically formalize this asymptotic convergence toward reference targets; @sec-appendix-control-clf details their theoretical foundation and how optimization pipelines unify stabilizing Lyapunov objectives with the safety barrier certificates this chapter develops in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.

[^fn-clf-tracking-convergence]: **Control Lyapunov Function**: A Lyapunov function certifies that an unforced system settles; a control Lyapunov function asks only that, at each state, some admissible input make it decrease. @artstein1983stabilization tied the existence of such a function to stabilizability by feedback, and @sontag1989universal gave an explicit formula that builds the stabilizing input from it. The control barrier function, defined later in this chapter, is its mirror image, keeping the state out of a region instead of pulling it toward a point, and when the two conflict the combined optimization relaxes convergence so that the barrier holds. \index{Control Lyapunov function!barrier counterpart}

This division of responsibilities cleanly separates trajectory tracking from safety enforcement. The low-level tracking controller focuses on driving the physical plant toward reference states, while the safety enforcer determines whether those references can be executed without violating invariant boundaries. The tracking error bound $\TrackingErrorBound$ bridges these subsystems by quantifying the spatial divergence between admitted commands and physical execution. Because environmental disturbances, unmodeled payload shifts, or thermal current derating can rapidly widen this error tube, safety architectures must continuously verify physical performance against contracted assumptions. The downstream stopping envelope accounts for this tracking tube alongside sensor latency, braking distance, and localization drift, ensuring that the physical robot remains safely buffered from surrounding hazards.

## Stopping Envelopes {#sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-stopping-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE FINISHED STOPPING BUDGET OF THE WAREHOUSE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: row 7 and aisle-speed prose below, @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget.
# │ Goal:    add the tracking inset (row 7), then choose the aisle speed that the
# │          finished budget allows.
# │ Show:    each row's term, value, running total, and remainder at the drive
# │          limit; the same terms at the aisle speed; the ceiling; the time rows;
# │          the missed-tick cost reused by the cycle list; the walking-person
# │          ceiling (moved from @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion); the
# │          base stall at the aisle speed (distance added, overrun past D_clear);
# │          the Delta_da allocation charged against the timing allowance and
# │          the reserve it leaves.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE fields; jerk bound = peak jerk of the reference C2
# │          polynomial at the drive limit (calc_c2_stop_suffix);
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance / _time (row 6, stop rows);
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity (ceilings, solved numerically);
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with tau + a/(2j) (closed-form
# │          cross-check above a^2/j); RM.intent_inference_latency, the
# │          computed prefill-plus-decode latency (time row).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import standard_gravity
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_stop_time,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
    calc_max_permitted_velocity,
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_free_space_expiry,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_jerk, fmt_magnitude, fmt_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementStoppingBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible, loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (excludes Delta_da)
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(
        millisecond
    )  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement-dispatch-admission, not yet measured)
    v_human = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 K)
    mu_inspected = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (deployed INT4 prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)
    t_stall = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (proposer stall before any brake)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_path = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus).to(millisecond)
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    # Jerk bound: the peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    v_plateau = (a_brake**2 / j_brake).to(meter / second)
    ramp_delay = (a_brake / (2 * j_brake)).to(millisecond)
    c2_drive = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_drive, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    c2_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)

    # Rows 1-7 at the drive limit, in book order
    brake_drive = (v_drive**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    onset_drive = (v_drive * t_act).to(millimeter)
    lease_drive = (v_drive * lease_path).to(millimeter)
    age_drive = (v_drive * t_age).to(millimeter)
    shape_drive = (c2_drive - brake_drive).to(millimeter)
    inset = eps_track.to(millimeter)
    run1 = brake_drive
    run2 = run1 + overhead
    run3 = run2 + onset_drive
    run4 = run3 + lease_drive
    run5 = run4 + age_drive
    run6 = run5 + shape_drive
    run7 = run6 + inset
    left = [
        (d_clear - run1).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run2).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run3).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run4).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run5).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run6).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run7).to(millimeter),
    ]

    # The same terms at the aisle speed
    brake_aisle = (v_aisle**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    onset_aisle = (v_aisle * t_act).to(millimeter)
    lease_aisle = (v_aisle * lease_path).to(millimeter)
    age_aisle = (v_aisle * t_age).to(millimeter)
    shape_aisle = (c2_aisle - brake_aisle).to(millimeter)
    total_aisle = (brake_aisle + overhead + onset_aisle + lease_aisle + age_aisle + shape_aisle + inset).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - total_aisle).to(millimeter)
    # Base stall: a last proposal that keeps authority for the stall instead of
    # the lease adds the extra delay's travel to the finished budget.
    stall_added = (v_aisle * (t_stall - t_lease)).to(millimeter)
    stall_breach = (total_aisle + stall_added - d_clear).to(millimeter)

    # Speed is the one free term: the subtotal ceiling before dispatch allocation
    ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    # Above a^2/j the S-curve is constant braking at a_brake with the delay lengthened by a/(2j)
    ceiling_closed = calc_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay + ramp_delay, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    total_check = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
        v_drive, tau_delay + ramp_delay, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(millimeter)
    # Operands of @eq-enforce-speed-ceiling for the napkin-math notebook
    tau_eff = (tau_delay + ramp_delay).to(millisecond)
    d_avail = (d_clear - delta_loc - delta_margin - eps_track).to(millimeter)
    a_tau = (a_brake * tau_eff).to(meter / second)
    a_tau_sq = (a_tau**2).to(meter**2 / second**2)
    two_a_d = (2 * a_brake * d_avail).to(meter**2 / second**2)
    root_term = ((a_tau_sq + two_a_d) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)
    ceiling_hand = (root_term - a_tau).to(meter / second)

    # Time rows (no distance added)
    # Free-space expiry abreast of the occluded rack end (@eq-mem-free-space-expiry):
    # the free depth is the hull-to-rack side clearance.
    belief_life = calc_free_space_expiry(AISLE.side_clearance, delta_loc, delta_margin, v_human).to(millisecond)
    missed_tick = (v_aisle * t_tick).to(millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    capture_to_admission_max = (t_age + t_latest).to(millisecond)
    capture_to_onset_max = (tau_delay + t_latest).to(millisecond)
    # Delta_da is not a term of tau_delay; the timing allowance pays for it.
    travel_da = (v_aisle * delta_da).to(millimeter)
    reserve_t = (t_latest - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    reserve_d = (spare - travel_da).to(millimeter)
    capture_to_onset = AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # rows 1-3 of @tbl-04-event-timing
    mu_min = (a_brake / standard_gravity).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_inspected = min(a_brake, (mu_inspected * standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2))
    # The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    ceiling_inspected = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_inspected, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)

    # Walking person: v tau + d_stop(v) + v_h (tau + T_stop(v)) + overhead = d_clear.
    # The S-curve's distance and time are not one polynomial in v, so MLSysIM solves it numerically.
    overhead_all = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: derived (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track)
    v_walk = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track, approach_velocity=v_human
    ).to(meter / second)
    d_walk = (
        v_walk * tau_delay
        + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake)
        + v_human * (tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_time(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake))
        + overhead_all
    ).to(meter)
    # Complete scenario roots charge dispatch travel once; moving humans also
    # close the gap during that interval. The inspected case remains an
    # optimistic all-weight traction screen, not a qualified braking bound.
    tau_complete = tau_delay + delta_da
    ceiling_complete = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_complete, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    ceiling_inspected_complete = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_complete, a_inspected, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    v_walk_complete = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_complete, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track, approach_velocity=v_human
    ).to(meter / second)
    complete_walk_distance = (
        v_walk_complete * tau_complete
        + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_walk_complete, a_brake, j_brake)
        + v_human * (tau_complete + calc_scurve_stop_time(v_walk_complete, a_brake, j_brake))
        + overhead_all
    ).to(meter)
    # Why the walking-person ceiling is so low: below a^2/j the jerk-limited stop never
    # reaches a_brake and lasts 2 sqrt(v/j), far longer than v/a, and the person walks
    # for the whole stop.
    t_stop_walk = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    t_stop_walk_const = (v_walk / a_brake).to(millisecond)
    brake_walk = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    closure_walk = (v_human * t_stop_walk).to(millimeter)
    # A reference polynomial rescaled to stop from v_walk at the full a_brake would need this jerk
    jerk_rescaled_walk = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_walk, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    # The same walking-person budget under constant-deceleration braking (no jerk bound):
    # v^2/2a + (tau + v_h/a) v + v_h tau + overhead - d_clear = 0, positive root
    _qa = 1 / (2 * a_brake)
    _qb = tau_delay + v_human / a_brake
    _qc = v_human * tau_delay + overhead_all - d_clear
    v_walk_const = ((-_qb + (_qb**2 - 4 * _qa * _qc) ** 0.5) / (2 * _qa)).to(meter / second)
    # Latency sensitivity of the static ceiling: 10 ms more pre-brake delay
    ceiling_plus10 = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay + 10 * millisecond, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    ceiling_drop_10ms = (ceiling - ceiling_plus10).to(millimeter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(run1.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, "Row 1 running total is 562.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run2.magnitude - 712.5) < 1e-6, "Row 2 running total is 712.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run3.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, "Row 3 running total is 742.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run4.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, "Row 4 running total is 835.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run5.magnitude - 912.9) < 1e-6, "Row 5 running total is 912.9 mm.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "The jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak.")
    check(v_aisle >= v_plateau and v_drive >= v_plateau, "Both budget speeds reach the deceleration bound (trapezoidal regime).")
    check(abs(run6.magnitude - 1123.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 6 running total is 1123.84 mm.")
    check(abs(run7.magnitude - 1163.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 7 running total is 1163.84 mm.")
    check(abs(total_check.magnitude - run7.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row 7 total must equal @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope at the drive limit.")
    check(abs(left[6].magnitude + 63.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 7 runs 63.84 mm past the clear distance.")
    check(abs(lease_path.magnitude - 62.0) < 1e-9, "Lease path is 62 ms.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-9, "tau_delay is 133.6 ms.")
    check(abs(ceiling.magnitude - ceiling_closed.magnitude) < 1e-9, "Numerical ceiling must match the closed form above a^2/j.")
    check(ceiling >= v_plateau, "The ceiling lies in the trapezoidal regime.")
    check(abs(ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Ceiling is 1.44 m/s.")
    check(abs(ceiling_hand.magnitude - ceiling.magnitude) < 1e-9, "The notebook's hand arithmetic must reproduce the ceiling.")
    check(abs(d_avail.magnitude - 910.0) < 1e-9, "Clearance left after the fixed allowances is 910 mm.")
    check(v_aisle < ceiling, "The chosen aisle speed must sit under the ceiling.")
    check(abs(total_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 1e-6, "Budget at 1.3 m/s is 968.99 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 1e-6, "Spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(stall_added.magnitude - 182.0) < 1e-6, "A 200 ms stall adds 182 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(stall_added > spare, "The stall's added travel exceeds the whole spare.")
    check(abs(stall_breach.magnitude - 50.9925) < 5e-3, "The stall runs 51.0 mm past the clear distance.")
    # 2026-09-28 (M1/M2): the deployed intent model is INT4; its full computed inference replaces the FP16 weight sweep.
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(t_intent > t_lease, "The intent inference cannot renew a chunk lease.")
    check(belief_life.magnitude == 0.0, "Abreast of the occluded rack end the free-space claim expires at capture.")
    check(abs(missed_tick.magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "One missed tick costs 1.3 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs(t_latest.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "The unallocated timing allowance is 100.8 ms at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(reserve_t.magnitude > 0 and reserve_d.magnitude > 0, "The Delta_da allocation must leave positive reserve.")
    check(abs((tau_delay + delta_da - capture_to_onset).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Capture to onset = tau_delay + Delta_da.")
    check(capture_to_onset < capture_to_onset_max, "The allocated capture-to-onset time must fall inside the latest onset.")
    check(
        abs((capture_to_onset_max - capture_to_admission_max - t_lease - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "Admission-to-onset must contain the lease, tick, bus, and drive onset exactly once.",
    )
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction premise is 0.204.")
    check(abs(ceiling_inspected.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor ceiling is 1.23 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_walk.magnitude - 0.2599) < 5e-5, f"Walking-person ceiling should be 0.260 m/s, got {v_walk}.")
    check(v_walk < v_plateau, "The walking-person stop never reaches the deceleration bound.")
    check(abs((d_walk - d_clear).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "At the walking-person ceiling the budget must fill the clear distance exactly.")
    check(abs(t_stop_walk.magnitude - 382.38) < 5e-2, "The jerk-limited stop from the walking-person ceiling lasts about 382 ms.")
    check(t_stop_walk > 2.9 * t_stop_walk_const, "Below a^2/j the jerk-limited stop lasts roughly three times a constant-deceleration stop.")
    check(closure_walk > 10 * brake_walk, "The person closes more than ten times the base's own braking travel.")
    check(jerk_rescaled_walk > 5 * j_brake, "Reaching a_brake from the walking-person ceiling would need several times the jerk bound.")
    check(abs(v_walk_const.magnitude - 0.6371) < 5e-4, "Without the jerk bound the walking-person ceiling would be 0.64 m/s.")
    check(ceiling_drop_10ms.magnitude > 0, "More pre-brake delay must lower the ceiling.")
    check(
        ceiling_complete < ceiling and ceiling_inspected_complete < ceiling_inspected and v_walk_complete < v_walk,
        "Positive dispatch allocation must lower each scenario root.",
    )
    check(v_aisle < ceiling_complete, "The dry aisle candidate must fit after dispatch allocation.")
    check(
        abs((complete_walk_distance - d_clear).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "The complete walking root charges closure throughout dispatch and stop.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling, precision=2)
    ceiling_complete_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_complete, precision=2)
    ceiling_inspected_complete_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_inspected_complete, precision=2)
    v_walk_complete_str = fmt_velocity(v_walk_complete, precision=2)
    ceiling_inspected_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_inspected, precision=2)
    v_walk_str = fmt_velocity(v_walk, precision=2)
    v_plateau_str = fmt_velocity(v_plateau, precision=2)
    v_human_str = fmt_velocity(v_human, precision=1)
    t_stop_walk_str = fmt_latency(round(t_stop_walk.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_stop_walk_const_str = fmt_latency(round(t_stop_walk_const.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    brake_walk_str = fmt_length(round(brake_walk.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    closure_walk_str = fmt_length(round(closure_walk.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    jerk_rescaled_walk_str = fmt_jerk(round(jerk_rescaled_walk.magnitude) * meter / second**3, precision=0)
    v_walk_const_str = fmt_velocity(v_walk_const, precision=2)
    ceiling_drop_10ms_str = fmt_int(ceiling_drop_10ms.magnitude)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    j_brake_str = fmt_jerk(j_brake, precision=2)
    ramp_delay_str = fmt_latency(ramp_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_eff_str = fmt_latency(tau_eff, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    d_avail_str = fmt_length(d_avail, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_mm_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    overhead_all_str = fmt_length(AISLE.fixed_overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    a_tau_str = fmt(a_tau.magnitude, precision=4)
    a_tau_sq_str = fmt(a_tau_sq.magnitude, precision=4)
    two_a_d_str = fmt(two_a_d.magnitude, precision=2)
    root_term_str = fmt(root_term.magnitude, precision=4)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    lease_path_str = fmt_latency(lease_path, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    belief_life_str = fmt_latency(belief_life, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    missed_tick_str = fmt_length(missed_tick, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    capture_to_admission_max_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_admission_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    capture_to_onset_max_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_onset_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    reserve_t_str = fmt_latency(reserve_t, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    reserve_d_str = fmt_length(reserve_d, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    capture_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(mu_inspected, precision=2)
    inset_str = fmt_length(inset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    run6_str = fmt_length(run6, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    run7_str = fmt_length(run7, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    over7_str = fmt_length(-left[6], unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    total_aisle_str = fmt_length(total_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_stall_str = fmt_latency(t_stall, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    stall_added_str = fmt_length(stall_added, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    stall_breach_str = fmt_length(stall_breach, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    # Table cells (the column headers carry mm)
    brake_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(brake_drive, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    overhead_value_str = fmt_magnitude(overhead, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    onset_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(onset_drive, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    lease_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(lease_drive, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    age_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(age_drive, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    shape_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(shape_drive, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    inset_value_str = fmt_magnitude(inset, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    run1_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run1, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run2_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run2, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run3_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run3, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run4_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run4, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run5_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run5, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run6_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run6, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    run7_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run7, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    left1_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[0], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left2_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[1], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left3_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[2], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left4_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[3], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left5_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[4], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left6_math = fmt_math(fmt_magnitude(left[5], millimeter, precision=2, commas=True))
    left7_math = fmt_math(fmt_magnitude(left[6], millimeter, precision=2, commas=True))
    brake_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(brake_aisle, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    onset_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(onset_aisle, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    lease_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(lease_aisle, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    age_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(age_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    shape_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(shape_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    total_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(total_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    spare_value_str = fmt_magnitude(spare, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    travel_da_value_str = fmt_magnitude(travel_da, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    reserve_d_value_str = fmt_magnitude(reserve_d, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
```

If the warehouse mobile manipulator approaches a rack end at its `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` mechanical drive limit when a coworker steps into the aisle, the delay before braking begins and the jerk-limited deceleration curve carry the base past the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clearance even before tracking error is counted. That rack-end crossing is the scene in which nearly every chapter since @sec-body has priced one stopping term: the body supplied braking and its fixed allowances, the Nervous System the lease path, perception the observation age, and planning the jerk-limited stop suffix that exceeded the rack-end clearance at the drive limit (@sec-planning-base-stopping-budget). The tracking bound of @sec-enforcement-handoff is the last spatial term. Every one of these terms serves the test that the first law, irreversibility (principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}), sets, $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$. The enforcer applies that test not as one calculation but as a set of states.

::: {#dfn-enforcement-stopping-envelope .callout-definition title="Stopping envelope"}

***Stopping envelope***\index{Stopping envelope!definition} is the set of plant states, parameterized by clearance and velocity along each degree of freedom, from which the resident emergency braking response, initiated after accounting for all worst-case delays, halts motion before reaching an obstacle boundary while preserving all localization, protective, and tracking margins.

1.  **Significance**: The envelope translates the abstract irreversibility requirement $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ into an actionable runtime velocity ceiling. When approaching a rack end, the warehouse mobile manipulator's envelope restricts forward velocity, with the stated dispatch allocation, to at most `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_complete_str`, substantially below its mechanical drive limit of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str`.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a static geometric keep-out zone that depends solely on position, the stopping envelope is a dynamic construct governed by speed, system latencies, and braking authority. A given physical clearance safely admits a slow approach while strictly forbidding a high-speed transit.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the stopping envelope as a static, precomputed boundary. In practice, carried payload mass, surface traction coefficients, and motor thermal limits continuously reshape this boundary; calculating safety margins from ideal datasheet decelerations severely overestimates stopping authority when the machine is heavily loaded.

:::

The stopping envelope is the machine's recoverable set, the states from which the resident stop still succeeds. @Sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states fixes the same boundary in time, as the commitment deadline past which momentum can carry the machine into an inevitable collision state. Velocity enters the recoverable set twice. Delay travel grows linearly with speed and braking travel quadratically, so a clearance that admits a slow approach forbids a fast one at the same position, and the enforcer must keep the machine inside the envelope on every tick, before a fault or an unmodeled disturbance can carry it out. The running calculation uses representative engineering limits; deployment requires each term to be qualified on the actual hardware.

The pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ of @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake already contains the enforcer's permission cycle, budgeted alongside the lease communication path in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing. One interval stays out of the spatial sum: the dispatch-to-admission delay $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, which @tbl-04-event-timing places between proposal dispatch and admission. The budget charges it instead against the timing allowance that the remaining clearance leaves (@sec-enforcement-composite-budget). What the spatial sum still lacks is the tracking error between the commanded reference and the actual plant.

The enforcer accounts for that error with the tracking bound $\TrackingErrorBound$, offsetting the baseline stopping distance of @eq-body-stopping-distance. It can admit a candidate reference trajectory only if the plant, which may lag that reference by up to $\TrackingErrorBound$, can still brake to a standstill within the available free distance $\ClearDistance$. Combining physical clearance, latency, and velocity yields the stopping subtotal before dispatch-to-admission travel is charged:
$$\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin + \TrackingErrorBound \le \ClearDistance$$ {#eq-enforce-stopping-envelope}
Here, $\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)$ represents the physical distance traversed during the braking maneuver from an initial speed $\SpeedAtDetection$. For idealized constant-deceleration braking, this term simplifies to $\SpeedAtDetection^2 / (2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration)$. Under realistic jerk-limited trajectory profiles, $\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)$ is governed by @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix, which incorporates the additional displacement accrued during finite jerk transitions. The term $\LocalizationBound$ denotes the localization uncertainty bound, while $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin$ provides an explicit protective safety cushion. The left-hand side sums the baseline stopping distance $\StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)$ from @eq-body-stopping-distance with the tracking inset $\TrackingErrorBound$.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The full stopping-distance model, tracking inset included, is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-stopping.
:::

For complete static-obstacle admission, the delay term uses $\PrebrakeDelay + \DispatchAdmissionInterval$ in place of $\PrebrakeDelay$; the resident stop and fixed allowances are unchanged. This inequality defines a conditional stopping subtotal in state space. Within this set, the accounted reaction latency and braking profile fit within the measured obstacle clearance; complete admission must also charge dispatch-to-admission travel. Operating outside this boundary violates the stopping reservation under the qualified model assumptions, though conservative engineering margins do not imply that an instantaneous collision is certain under all conceivable emergency maneuvers. Per-tick enforcement must maintain this stopping reservation over the entire control epoch until the next validated command can take effect, rather than merely verifying instantaneous feasibility at the sample instant.

Whenever a proposed trajectory requires a stopping distance in @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope that exceeds the measured clearance along the current heading, the enforcer rejects the command. Because the robot moves directionally, the stopping envelope is anisotropic\index{Stopping envelope!Anisotropy}. Heading dictates which obstacles threaten forward travel and consume braking clearance, while localization uncertainty and the robot's swept geometric volume demand clearance margins around the entire perimeter.

### Sizing the composite stopping budget {#sec-enforcement-composite-budget}

Omitting any single interval during which the base keeps moving before or during a stop, or evaluating those intervals under mismatched operating conditions, admits transit speeds that overrun the physical boundary when all delays coincide. The composite stopping budget therefore reserves clearance for every interval in the arrest sequence: sensor transduction lag, compute scheduling delays, actuator engagement, the deceleration profile, and tracking divergence, each evaluated under the same worst-case operating conditions.

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the tracking bound of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.inset_str` is the final spatial term. At the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit, the matched stop suffix had already pushed the cumulative requirement to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.run6_str`, past the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance; that is the deficit @sec-planning-base-stopping-budget left open. The tracking inset carries the total to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.run7_str`, an overshoot of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.over7_str` beyond the physical boundary.

The $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ stop suffix replaces idealized constant deceleration ($\SpeedAtDetection^2 / 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$) with the jerk-limited S-curve of @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix, governed by the peak jerk limit $\JerkLimit =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake_str`. Planning stipulated that bound from the reference $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ polynomial rather than measuring it; the S-curve is the stop the MCU actually runs, and the polynomial supplies only its jerk bound. Because both operating velocities reach the peak deceleration threshold, @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix models this maneuver by adding the displacement of half a jerk ramp:
$$\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) = \frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration} + \SpeedAtDetection\,\frac{\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{2 \JerkLimit}.$$
Because this smoothly shaped stop consumes more clearance than discontinuous full-torque braking, the admissible transit speed must be read from the finished budget rather than from the constant-deceleration estimate.

Velocity remains the single operational variable the control architecture can dynamically modulate. Above the characteristic velocity threshold $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration^2/\JerkLimit =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_plateau_str`, the finite jerk ramps function equivalently to an added delay of $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration/(2\JerkLimit)$ prior to braking at constant deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$. Under these conditions, the pre-dispatch **speed ceiling**\index{Speed ceiling!stopping envelope} keeps the form of @eq-body-velocity-ceiling, the positive root of the stopping inequality at equality. The jerk ramps lengthen the pre-brake delay to an effective delay, and the tracking bound comes off the available braking distance:
$$\SpeedBound = -\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\EffectiveBrakingDelay + \sqrt{(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\EffectiveBrakingDelay)^2 + 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\InsetAvailableBrakingDistance}, \qquad \EffectiveBrakingDelay = \PrebrakeDelay + \frac{\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{2\JerkLimit}, \qquad \InsetAvailableBrakingDistance = \ClearDistance - \LocalizationBound - \ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \TrackingErrorBound$$ {#eq-enforce-speed-ceiling}
Below $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration^2/\JerkLimit$, the deceleration trajectory never reaches the peak limit $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$, rendering stopping distance non-quadratic in velocity; in this low-speed regime, MLSysIM evaluates @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope via numerical root-finding. Notebook \ref{nbk-enforcement-speed-ceiling} computes this ceiling for the mobile manipulator approaching the aisle rack end.

::: {#nbk-enforcement-speed-ceiling .callout-notebook title="The ceiling the budget sets"}

**Problem**: The warehouse mobile manipulator approaches the rack end with rows 1 to 7 of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget accounted, before dispatch-to-admission travel. What is the highest speed at which the jerk-limited stop still fits the clear distance, and how much clearance does a candidate aisle speed of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` leave?

**Variables**:

* $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` (Illustrative; clear distance at the rack end).
* $\LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_loc_str` $+$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_margin_str` (Illustrative localization bound; chosen protective clearance), and $\TrackingErrorBound =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.inset_str` (Illustrative; the qualification target of @sec-enforcement-handoff).
* $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_brake_str` (Illustrative; credible loaded deceleration on a dry floor) and $\JerkLimit =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake_str` (Derived; the peak jerk of the reference $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ polynomial).
* $\PrebrakeDelay =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` (Derived; observation age plus lease path plus brake onset, excluding $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$).
* Drive limit `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` (Illustrative).

**Math**: The fixed allowances leave $\InsetAvailableBrakingDistance =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_mm_str` $-$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.overhead_all_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_avail_str`. The jerk ramps lengthen the delay to $\EffectiveBrakingDelay =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` $+$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ramp_delay_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_eff_str`, so $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\EffectiveBrakingDelay =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_str` m/s. Under the square root of @eq-enforce-speed-ceiling, $(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\EffectiveBrakingDelay)^2 =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_sq_str` and $2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration{}\InsetAvailableBrakingDistance =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.two_a_d_str` (both in m²/s²), whose sum has root `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.root_term_str` m/s; subtracting `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_str` m/s gives the ceiling. At `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` the terms of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget sum to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.total_aisle_str`, and the remainder divided by the speed is the timing allowance.

**Result**: The pre-dispatch ceiling is $\SpeedBound =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_str`, below the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit. The candidate aisle speed leaves `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` of spare, equivalent to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` of unallocated delay.

**Systems insight**: The irreversibility requirement $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$, rather than motor electrical capability, dictates the operating speed. Running at the nominal drive limit violates the verified spatial budget, and the speed ceiling shifts strictly through the parameters governing the quadratic root and effective latency $\EffectiveBrakingDelay$: available clearance, qualified braking deceleration, fixed margins, and end-to-end transport lag. Any latency introduced by downstream processing directly consumes the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` timing allowance, which cannot be arbitrarily replenished.

:::

The candidate transit speed, `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str`, sits below that ceiling, and its `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` margin is the only clearance left to absorb unmodeled pipeline delays or to serve as a reserve. That margin is narrow relative to the failure modes it must absorb. If chunk lease enforcement were entrusted to a non-real-time host operating system, an upstream planning stall lasting `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_stall_str` instead of the nominal `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.lease_ms_str` lease would inject `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.stall_added_str` of unbraked displacement, causing the base to overrun the rack clearance by `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.stall_breach_str`. This hazard shows why lease termination must be autonomously enforced by dedicated microcontroller hardware directly gating motor power (@sec-enforcement-authority-refuse).

The observation-age term ends at dispatch, and the chunk lease begins at admission, so the interval between them, $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, belongs to neither. The complete operational delay therefore expands to $\AdmissionInclusivePrebrakeDelay = \PrebrakeDelay + \DispatchAdmissionInterval$, requiring an additional spatial reservation of $\SpeedAtDetection\DispatchAdmissionInterval$. This phase encompasses any remaining neural inference, safety envelope projection, and inter-process communication; pipelined or overlapping stages must be budgeted carefully to avoid double-counting. A newly arrived sensor observation updates this budget only when the hardware pipeline delivers and validates it prior to actuation. Laid out on one time axis (@fig-12-capture-to-onset), the observation age ends at dispatch, the dispatch-to-admission interval follows, and the lease, one tick, one bus cycle, and drive onset bring the base to brake onset. A travel row beneath converts each interval into millimeters at the candidate aisle speed.

At this candidate speed, dividing the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` spare distance by the speed yields `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` of unallocated timing allowance. Added to the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_age_str` observation age, that allowance places the latest admission after capture at `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_admission_max_str`. Added to the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay, it places the latest brake onset after capture at `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_onset_max_str`. The dispatch-to-admission interval spends part of that allowance and leaves whatever remains as the reserve; because operating right at these boundaries spends all available clearance, the figures are qualification constraints rather than performance claims. The budget carries forward the allocation that the placement chapter makes for this interval (@sec-placement-dispatch-admission), $\DispatchAdmissionInterval =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_da_str` for the partitioned compute pipeline. That allocation consumes `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.travel_da_str` of the spatial margin, leaves a cushion of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_t_str` (`{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_d_str` of distance), and puts total latency from capture to brake onset at `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_onset_str`. Because that allocation is an engineering budget rather than a measurement, an instrumented campaign with hardware timestamps must confirm it before the vehicle can be certified at this speed. Read row by row (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget, @fig-enforcement-stopping-budget), the terms through observation age fit inside the clear distance at the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit, whereas the jerk-limited stop (row 6) carries the total past the line and the tracking inset (row 7) widens the breach. At the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, those same terms stop `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` short of the line and still leave a `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_d_str` reserve once dispatch-to-admission travel is charged.

| Row | Added in                             | Term                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |                                        At drive limit (mm) |                                  Running total (mm) |                        Left of $\ClearDistance$ (mm) |                                        At aisle speed (mm) |
|----:|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------------:|-----------------------------------------------------:|-----------------------------------------------------------:|
|   1 | @sec-body-kinetic-momentum           | Braking, $\SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$                                                                                                                                                                  | `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.brake_drive_value_str` | `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.run1_value_str` | `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.left1_value_str` | `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.brake_aisle_value_str` |
