In computational graph terms, relative degree is the graph distance, counted in time-integrator nodes, between the commanded control input $\ControlInput$ and the barrier certificate $\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState)$. If an engineer defines a safety certificate purely as geometric clearance, $\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState) = \ObstaclePosition - \RobotPosition \ge 0$, the commanded actuation is separated from position by two successive integrations:
$$\text{Actuation } \ActuatorEffort \xrightarrow{\int \frac{1}{\Mass} d\TimeInstant} \text{Velocity } \RobotApproachVelocity \xrightarrow{\int d\TimeInstant} \text{Position } \RobotPosition$$
This two-stage integration cascade establishes relative degree $\BarrierRelativeDegree = 2$. Taking the first time derivative of clearance yields the closing velocity, $\BarrierFunctionRate = -\RobotApproachVelocity$, which contains no control input whatsoever ($\LieDerivativeAlongControl(\MechanicalPlantState) = \text{JVP}(\BarrierFunction, \MechanicalPlantState, \ControlAffineInputField(\MechanicalPlantState)) = \ZeroVector$). Because the control authority JVP evaluates to zero, motor torque has zero instantaneous authority over the rate of barrier decay. At the boundary of the safe set ($\BarrierFunction = 0$), enforcing forward invariance $\BarrierFunctionRate \ge -\ClassKFunction(0) = 0$ requires $-\RobotApproachVelocity \ge 0 \implies \RobotApproachVelocity \le 0$. Halting a moving system instantaneously would require infinite deceleration and unbounded torque ($\ActuatorEffort = -\infty$). Applying this first-derivative condition to position alone provides no torque constraint before the geometric boundary. Higher-order barrier formulations can retain a position constraint and differentiate until the input appears; this chapter instead incorporates the stopping distance explicitly.

To restore nonzero control authority ($\LieDerivativeAlongControl \neq \ZeroVector$), the barrier certificate must explicitly incorporate kinetic energy and braking limits. For an approaching arm joint, let $\AngularClearance = \ToolClearanceDistance / \LeverArmLength$ represent the remaining angular clearance, $\JointAngularSpeed > 0$ the approach speed, $\EffectiveJointInertia \JointAngularAcceleration = \CommandedJointTorque + \JointBiasTorque$ the joint dynamics, and $\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration$ a validated lower bound on net available angular braking deceleration. Adopting the linear class-$\Glyph{\mathcal{K}}$ function $\ClassKFunction(\BarrierFunction) = \LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction$, where $\LinearBarrierDecayRate > 0$ is a constant approach-rate gain, the **kinetic barrier certificate** is:
$$\BarrierFunction(\AngularClearance,\JointAngularSpeed)=\AngularClearance-\frac{\JointAngularSpeed^2}{2\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration}.$$ {#eq-enforce-kinetic-barrier}
Differentiating $\BarrierFunction(\AngularClearance,\JointAngularSpeed)$ along the joint dynamics yields $\BarrierFunctionRate = \LieDerivativeAlongDrift + \LieDerivativeAlongControl\,\CommandedJointTorque$, where $\LieDerivativeAlongControl = -\frac{\JointAngularSpeed}{\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration} \ne 0$ for any nonzero approach speed $\JointAngularSpeed > 0$. Because commanded torque $\CommandedJointTorque$ appears directly in this first time derivative with a nonzero coefficient, the kinetic barrier achieves **relative degree one** ($\BarrierRelativeDegree = 1$). Actuator commands now exert immediate control authority across the causal boundary. Enforcing the forward-invariance condition $\BarrierFunctionRate + \LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction \ge 0$ isolates the admissible torque into an explicit affine half-space constraint:[^fn-math-kinetic-derivation]
$$\CommandedJointTorque\le-\JointBiasTorque+\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration\left(\frac{\LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction}{\JointAngularSpeed}-1\right),\qquad -\JointTorqueLimit\le\CommandedJointTorque\le\JointTorqueLimit.$$ {#eq-enforce-kinetic-torque}
In this sign convention, positive angular velocity $\JointAngularSpeed$, positive gravitational bias $\JointBiasTorque$, and positive motor torque $\CommandedJointTorque$ all act downward toward the workstation so that clearance shrinks at rate $\AngularClearanceRate = -\JointAngularSpeed$, and a negative upper bound on $\CommandedJointTorque$ in @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque therefore sets a minimum magnitude on the upward braking torque $-\CommandedJointTorque$ that the motor must apply against gravity. This condition defines the linear half-space $\BarrierConstraintNormal(\MechanicalPlantState)^\top \ControlInput \le \BarrierConstraintBound(\MechanicalPlantState)$ solved by the control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP) filter developed next, with the half-space normal and scalar threshold determined directly by the Jacobian-vector products: $\BarrierConstraintNormal(\MechanicalPlantState)^\top = -\LieDerivativeAlongControl(\MechanicalPlantState)$ and $\BarrierConstraintBound(\MechanicalPlantState) = \LieDerivativeAlongDrift(\MechanicalPlantState) + \LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState)$. At standstill ($\JointAngularSpeed = 0$), the microcontroller firmware applies a separate static acceleration and position-hold check to prevent division by zero.[^fn-cbf-standstill-guard]

[^fn-math-kinetic-derivation]: **Kinetic barrier directional derivative chain rule**: Evaluating $\BarrierFunctionRate(\AngularClearance, \JointAngularSpeed) = \frac{\partial \BarrierFunction}{\partial \AngularClearance}\AngularClearanceRate + \frac{\partial \BarrierFunction}{\partial \JointAngularSpeed}\JointAngularAcceleration$ with $\AngularClearanceRate = -\JointAngularSpeed$ and $\JointAngularAcceleration = (\CommandedJointTorque + \JointBiasTorque)/\EffectiveJointInertia$ yields $\BarrierFunctionRate = (-\JointAngularSpeed - \frac{\JointAngularSpeed\JointBiasTorque}{\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration}) - \frac{\JointAngularSpeed}{\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration}\CommandedJointTorque = \LieDerivativeAlongDrift(\AngularClearance,\JointAngularSpeed) + \LieDerivativeAlongControl(\AngularClearance,\JointAngularSpeed)\CommandedJointTorque$. Substituting into $\BarrierFunctionRate + \LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction \ge 0$ and rearranging produces $\frac{\JointAngularSpeed(\CommandedJointTorque + \JointBiasTorque)}{\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration} \le \LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction - \JointAngularSpeed$. Multiplying by the positive factor $\frac{\EffectiveJointInertia\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration}{\JointAngularSpeed}$ and subtracting the bias yields @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque.

[^fn-cbf-standstill-guard]: **Standstill velocity thresholding**: In microcontroller firmware, floating-point evaluation of $\frac{\LinearBarrierDecayRate \BarrierFunction}{\JointAngularSpeed}$ is explicitly guarded by a velocity threshold $\StandstillSpeedThreshold$: when $|\JointAngularSpeed| \le \StandstillSpeedThreshold$, the kinetic barrier is bypassed in favor of a static acceleration or position-hold bound, preventing floating-point division by zero and NaN exceptions in the sub-millisecond loop.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-kinetic-barrier
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KINETIC BARRIER ON THE MACHINE'S DESCENDING ARM JOINT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the loaded-arm paragraph immediately below (@eq-enforce-kinetic-torque).
# │ Goal:    evaluate the torque ceiling of the kinetic barrier at three clearances.
# │ Show:    alpha, h at 110 mm, the h = 0 clearance, and the braking torque demanded.
# │ How:     reuses the joint scenario of EnforcementAuthorityLoss (RM.arm torque).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_torque, check

class KineticBarrierArm:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    inertia = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.inertia  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    bias = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    torque_limit = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit  # category: datasheet
    speed = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed  # rad/s; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    radius = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.link_length  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    gamma = 10.0 / second  # scenario assumption; category: chosen (barrier gain)
    clear_far = 110 * millimeter  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    clear_near = 70 * millimeter  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = ((torque_limit - bias) / inertia).to(1 / second**2)
    stop_angle = (speed**2 / (2 * alpha)).to("dimensionless")
    clear_zero = (radius * stop_angle).to(millimeter)
    angle_far = (clear_far / radius).to("dimensionless")
    h_far = angle_far - stop_angle
    h_near = (clear_near / radius).to("dimensionless") - stop_angle
    ceiling_far = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (gamma * h_far / speed - 1)).to(newton * meter)
    ceiling_zero = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (0 - 1)).to(newton * meter)
    ceiling_near = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (gamma * h_near / speed - 1)).to(newton * meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(alpha.magnitude - 7.25) < 1e-9, "Net braking headroom gives 7.25 rad/s^2.")
    check(abs(ceiling_far.magnitude + 80.078125) < 1e-9, "At 110 mm the barrier demands at least 80.1 N·m of braking.")
    check(abs(ceiling_zero.magnitude + torque_limit.magnitude) < 1e-9, "At h = 0 the barrier demands the full peak torque.")
    check(-ceiling_near > torque_limit, "At 70 mm the demanded braking torque exceeds the joint's peak torque.")
    # margin_barrier_braking_demand_knee.svg and its fig-alt hand-type 80.1, 87, 89.1 N·m and 79.45, 70, 110 mm.
    check(abs(-ceiling_near.magnitude - 89.1) < 0.05, "At 70 mm the barrier demands 89.1 N·m.")
    check(abs(clear_zero.magnitude - 79.45) < 0.01, "The barrier's zero set sits at 79.45 mm of tool clearance.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha.magnitude, precision=2)
    gamma_str = fmt(gamma.magnitude, precision=0)
    angle_far_str = fmt(angle_far.magnitude, precision=4)
    h_far_str = fmt(h_far.magnitude, precision=4)
    clear_far_str = fmt_length(clear_far, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    clear_zero_str = fmt_length(clear_zero, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    clear_near_str = fmt_length(clear_near, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    brake_far_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_far, precision=1)
    brake_zero_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_zero, precision=0)
    brake_near_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_near, precision=1)
```

Applying this kinetic barrier to the descending-arm parameters from @sec-enforcement-exhausted-authority sets concrete torque ceilings across the approach. The moment of inertia is $\EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.inertia_str`. The gravitational bias torque is $\JointBiasTorque =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias_str`, directed toward the workstation. The actuator saturation limit is $|\CommandedJointTorque| \le$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit_str`, so the net angular braking deceleration is $\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration = (\JointTorqueLimit - \JointBiasTorque) / \EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.alpha_str` $\text{rad/s}^2$. The link lever arm is $\LeverArmLength =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.link_length_str`, the approach speed is $\JointAngularSpeed =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed_str` $\text{rad/s}$, and the barrier gain is $\LinearBarrierDecayRate =$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.gamma_str` $\text{s}^{-1}$. These are stipulated joint-level dynamics that deployment must calibrate on the actual arm. At `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_far_str` of tool clearance from the workstation surface, the angular clearance is $\AngularClearance =$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.angle_far_str` $\text{rad}$ and the barrier certificate evaluates to $\BarrierFunction =$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.h_far_str` $\text{rad}$, so substituting into @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque requires the joint to deliver at least `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_far_str` of counteracting braking torque. Most of that demand is not deceleration at all, because the first `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias_str` merely cancels gravity to keep the joint from speeding up and only the remainder slows it, which is why a joint still outside its zero set already asks for most of its peak torque. At `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_zero_str`, the system reaches the zero set ($\BarrierFunction = 0$) where the barrier demands `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_zero_str`, the motor's full peak torque capacity. If clearance degrades further to `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_near_str`, the inequality demands `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_near_str`, which exceeds peak actuator limits and places the state outside the control-admissible viable set. There, under these scalar dynamics, fixed bias, and instantaneous maximum-braking assumptions, no controller initiated at that point can prevent contact.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_barrier_braking_demand_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Line of the braking torque the barrier demands against tool clearance, falling as clearance grows. A dot at 110 millimeters reads 80.1 newton meters. The line meets a red dashed line at the joint's 87 newton meter peak at 79.45 millimeters, where h equals 0, and a red dot at 70 millimeters reads 89.1 newton meters, above the peak, in a shaded red region."}

*Inside `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_zero_str` of clearance the barrier asks for more braking than the joint has.*
:::

Physical robotic hardware provides neither perfectly continuous state feedback nor instantaneous torque response. Stator current rise times, fieldbus jitter, and drivetrain mechanical compliance delay and soften corrective torque delivery. To guarantee safety under these real-world non-idealities, the runtime enforcer evaluates the barrier certificate against an inset boundary that explicitly accounts for the worst-case stopping deficit induced by hardware latency and compliant dynamics. This initiates corrective filtering earlier along the trajectory.

This kinetic barrier construction follows directly from rigid-body braking mechanics. For the stipulated scalar approach with exact dynamics, fixed bias, instantaneous effort, and no omitted margins, its zero level set represents the exact boundary of states from which maximum allowable braking stops the joint before collision: the **viability kernel**\index{Viability kernel} [@aubin1991viability] of a double integrator subject to actuator saturation. Among collision-free states, the kernel's complement is the set of inevitable collision states defined in @sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states. With a conservative available lower bound instead of exact maximum braking, the same construction supplies a sufficient stopping set rather than the exact kernel. The resulting torque requirement remains compatible with the stipulated actuator limits. At $\BarrierFunction = 0$, the inequality in @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque demands exactly $-\JointTorqueLimit$, and for all $\BarrierFunction > 0$ the demand is strictly less restrictive, ensuring that at least one admissible control command exists everywhere within the safe set. Actuator feasibility across the entire set, not merely the calculus of the derivative, is what qualifies $\BarrierFunction(\AngularClearance, \JointAngularSpeed)$ as a valid barrier certificate under input constraints.

This identical principle governs autonomous base navigation. The mobile base certificate $\MobileBaseBarrierFunction(\ClearDistance, \SpeedAtDetection) = \ClearDistance - [\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin + \TrackingErrorBound]$ is nonnegative precisely when the stopping subtotal in @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope fits the clearance. The operational certificate must additionally subtract the dispatch-to-admission travel before granting permission. Both constructions reserve the motion needed to stop. A nonnegative stopping reservation alone does not establish forward invariance; the sampled implementation must also preserve that reservation under its qualified state, effort, and timing bounds. The single-joint arm derivation omits latency and localization margins temporarily only to isolate the mechanics of relative degree.

When complex nonlinear dynamics prevent closed-form analytical solutions for the viability kernel, **Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability**\index{Hamilton-Jacobi reachability}[^fn-hj-reachability-games] computes the boundary numerically as the zero level set of an optimal control value function [@mitchell2005time; @bansal2017hamilton]. The resulting tabulated lookup surface serves as the runtime barrier certificate, with its spatial gradient defining the half-space normal for real-time filtering. Because state-space grid discretization scales exponentially with dimensionality, HJ reachability lookup tables are best suited for decoupled, low-dimensional subsystems such as a single revolute joint or the longitudinal tracking channel of a mobile base.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The Hamilton-Jacobi value function and its differential-game formulation are developed in @sec-appendix-control-hj-reachability.
:::

[^fn-hj-reachability-games]: **Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability**: Originating in the zero-sum differential game formulations of @isaacs1965differential, reachability analysis frames safety as a game between a control policy and a worst-case adversarial disturbance. The resulting safe set contains precisely those states from which the controller can guarantee safety against any bounded disturbance trajectory. Consequently, an HJ reachability table is inherently robust but conservative, and its safety guarantee holds only within the assumed disturbance envelope. \index{Hamilton-Jacobi reachability!differential games}

A barrier certificate specifies which actuator commands preserve forward invariance, but it does not specify how the runtime safety path should handle an uncertified proposal. When a candidate command violates the half-space constraint, the enforcer must choose whether to project the command onto the boundary of admissible inputs, reject it in favor of a precomputed emergency braking trajectory, or maintain the previously certified setpoint. This intervention policy determines how mathematical barrier constraints translate into real-time authority over the motor drives.

## Refusing Proposals and Enforcing State Invariants {#sec-enforcement-authority-refuse}

A trajectory chunk arrives from the application processor on schedule, properly framed, and bearing a fresh evidence timestamp, yet one of its constituent joint setpoints would accelerate the arm directly into a steel rack upright. Nothing in the incoming packet payload marks that setpoint as erroneous. The permission path therefore grants zero executive authority to an incoming learned command until that proposal passes the configured state, input, freshness, and stopping-clearance checks. This is the third law, **proposal is not permission** (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}), executed deterministically one `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` tick at a time. Rather than assuming that a learned proposal satisfies stability criteria, actuator limits, or stopping guarantees, the permission path treats every incoming vector strictly as an advisory candidate.

The resident controller and output selector translate this principle of refusal into deterministic execution. The resident controller maintains a fallback response qualified for the current machine state, while the selector determines whether to admit an incoming candidate, apply a feasible correction, or transfer authority directly to that resident response. Rejecting an incoming candidate does not instantaneously abort the command currently driving the plant. Instead, the active command continues running so long as its own evidence timestamp, lease deadline, tracking error bound, and stopping reservation remain valid.

Under this architecture, the upstream neural policy never commands the physical plant directly. Its proposals reach the safety MCU through the board link and seqlock mailbox, with no addressable memory shared between the two compute domains. Each admitted chunk drives the plant only under a chunk lease, a hardware-enforced dead-man permission[^fn-deadman-control-lease] that lapses unless a fresh, validated proposal renews it. A trajectory chunk arrives as a horizon of $\ActionChunkHorizon$ waypoints, and the admission filter inspects all $\ActionChunkHorizon$ points against reach, velocity, and stopping-reservation constraints before permitting the first waypoint to execute. On each subsequent control tick, the enforcer re-evaluates the specific setpoint scheduled for execution against live sensor telemetry. If the enforcer projects a setpoint on a single tick, it does not rewrite the chunk's downstream waypoints. Instead, the safety MCU reports the intervention upstream, requiring the policy to replan from the actual, corrected state rather than resuming execution along a trajectory computed for a state the machine never reached.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The seqlock mailbox that hands proposals to the permission path is established in @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges.
:::

If the proposal remains fresh, the physical machine state resides within the qualified stopping region, and the tracking error satisfies $\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\| \le \TrackingErrorBound$, the output selector permits the proposal (or its minimally projected variant $\CertifiedControlAction$) to drive the actuators. Conversely, if the chunk lease expires without renewal, tracking error breaches the tolerance bound, no admissible command satisfies instantaneous physical constraints, or the active command endangers physical boundaries beyond the corrective capacity of projection, the output selector revokes permission and unilaterally engages the baseline safety controller. The upstream neural policy is not consulted, cannot negotiate, and possesses no hardware mechanism to override the selector's decision.

[^fn-deadman-control-lease]: **Dead-Man Control**: Early electric locomotives incorporated a spring-loaded dead-man handle that the operator had to depress continuously; releasing the handle (if the driver lost consciousness, for example) interrupted tractive power and engaged the mechanical brakes. System safety arose from the cessation of action rather than the transmission of an explicit fault message. The chunk lease applies the same principle in software. The host must actively renew its permission, ensuring that an upstream processor too damaged to command a stop is inherently incapable of renewing execution authority. \index{Dead-man control!chunk lease}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-latch-filter
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE LATCH APPROACH AS THE FILTERING CASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the filter-vs.-veto paragraph immediately below; the record's
# │          approach-ceiling paragraph cites the same speeds.
# │ Goal:    give the chapter's first projection on the machine.
# │ Show:    the chunk policy's proposed approach and the target-ODD approach.
# │ How:     AISLE latch fields (the same ones EnforcementRecordMachine loads).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_velocity, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementLatchFilter:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (target-ODD approach)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    speed_ratio = (v_latch_high / v_latch).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "The policy proposes 0.10 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_latch.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "The target-ODD approach is 0.03 m/s.")
    check(speed_ratio > 1.0, "The proposed approach is faster than the evidence covers.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch_high, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch, precision=2)
```

When a proposal conflicts with physical constraints, the enforcer chooses between filtering and vetoing the command. Filtering applies when the proposal is structurally sound and a nearby admissible control action preserves the policy's underlying intent. Consider the manipulator arm approaching a spring-latched cage door when the chunk policy proposes approaching the strike plate at `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_high_str`. The door zone admits only the guarded approach speed of `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_str` defined by the target operational design domain (ODD), the velocity envelope validated across empirical trials and demonstration datasets. The faster proposal therefore fails on both evidential and physical grounds. It fails on evidence, because no trial or demonstration sampled that speed. It also fails on physics, because the contact analysis of @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact shows that at that speed the force on the plate at brake onset nearly reaches the latch limit, leaving a stop that demands far harder arm deceleration than the guarded approach needs. Consequently, the enforcer preserves the approach trajectory's target and spatial direction, projecting only its scalar speed down to the `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_str` limit. The least-change quadratic program\index{Quadratic programming} formulated in @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention solves this projection in real time alongside the half-space constraints derived by a control barrier function\index{Control barrier function}.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The evaluation record's target ODD boundary, sampled at the guarded approach speed, is established in @sec-evaluation-logs.
:::

Filtering must account for momentum alongside position, ensuring that the actuators retain sufficient control authority to bring the machine to a complete stop before available clearance vanishes (@sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission). In the latch example, scalar speed projection preserves both the goal and the approach direction. In a coupled joint-torque filter, however, a correction can alter the end-effector trajectory through task space; such modification remains permissible only when the revised motion satisfies dynamic continuity constraints and remains task-admissible. Conversely, a structurally invalid proposal (a discontinuous jump in commanded position, an acceleration profile beyond peak motor torque, or a trajectory pointed directly into an immovable obstacle) indicates that perception or inference has entered an unmodeled failure mode. Projecting an ungrounded candidate onto the nearest admissible boundary would execute arbitrary motion unrelated to any coherent task intent. Under these conditions, the enforcer exercises an outright veto. The selector permits the active command to finish only if that command continues to satisfy its own validity checks; otherwise, it immediately transfers authority to a prequalified local fallback.

Both filtering and veto operate strictly at runtime; offline training cannot substitute for either mechanism. Penalty terms, barrier losses, and reward shaping bias the policy distribution during training, but they cannot mathematically bound what the deployed neural network will emit in edge cases. The **statistical safety fallacy**\index{Statistical safety fallacy} conflates a bound on expected violation cost with an absolute guarantee across every execution trace. A constrained reinforcement learning\index{Constrained reinforcement learning} objective such as $\mathbb{E}[\text{cost}] \le \ExpectedCostLimit$ constrains only the ensemble mean, leaving open the possibility of catastrophic tail events during individual rollouts. Formal neural-network verification can establish provable output bounds over bounded input sets [@katz2017reluplex], and closed-loop verification can combine those bounds with plant models. Formal proofs nevertheless remain vulnerable to reality gaps: unmodeled friction, sensor latency, non-deterministic scheduling, or actuator saturation outside the proof's operational assumptions will invalidate the guarantee. The permission path therefore verifies every candidate control vector at the hardware actuation boundary, regardless of the optimization objective used during training. When an incoming proposal is safe, the verification check is transparent, allowing learned sensorimotor competence to pass directly to the motor drives without alteration.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Why training-time penalties cannot bound the actions a deployed policy emits is established in @sec-boundary-fallacies-pitfalls.
:::

The chunk lease, `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.lease_ms_str` on this machine, bounds upstream execution authority during a host stall or scheduling delay, provided the local timer, selector, sensing, and actuation paths survive. In addition to the lease, a dedicated `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_rate_hz_str` $\text{Hz}$ host heartbeat monitors basic link viability with a `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_timeout_ms_str` silence timeout. The safety MCU executes its deterministic `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.loop_rate_str` control loop, servicing a local `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.self_watchdog_ms_str` hardware watchdog timer only after successfully completing an entire cycle; an independent hardware trip circuit supervises MCU power and clock integrity. If either the host heartbeat or the chunk lease expires, the safety MCU revokes proposal permissions and engages a deterministic, state-matched fallback from the responses that @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder defines, assuming reserved clearance and actuator braking capacities remain sufficient. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, if a proposer renews its lease and subsequently stalls, mechanical braking begins within `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.renewal_to_onset_ms_str` of the last valid renewal. This lease-expiry scenario assumes the underlying heartbeat remains active even as valid proposals cease; a total host operating-system freeze trips the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_timeout_ms_str` heartbeat timeout even earlier. If a worker steps out from behind a warehouse rack, the sensor capture latency of the camera frame that first revealed the obstacle adds directly to this renewal-to-onset delay, and @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes carries this cumulative latency directly into the admission check.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The lease, heartbeat, and self-watchdog timers, and why a heartbeat cannot renew a lease, are established in @sec-nervous-supervisory-timers.
:::

Severing upstream authority requires an unambiguously defined physical response at the lowest hardware interface. The zero-command floor\index{Zero-command floor} defines the default physical state enforced when active software control terminates, but commanding 'zero' produces drastically different dynamics depending on the actuator topology. Injecting zero current into a low-friction, direct-drive actuator allows a gravity-loaded manipulator arm to drop freely unless a mechanical brake or counterweight holds the link. Conversely, commanding zero velocity to a stiff position-controlled servo can demand infinite acceleration and trigger violent inertial transients. As detailed in @sec-body-unpowered-states, an unpowered drive drops into one of three hardware states: unconstrained coasting, phase-short dynamic braking\index{Dynamic braking}, or mechanical locking via spring-applied brakes. The system architect must ensure that the commanded fallback matches both the instantaneous kinetic state and the physical capabilities of the surviving hardware.

Proposal rejection is a continuous, steady-state operating decision rather than an exceptional emergency trip. The enforcer must evaluate every invariant and execute its selected fallback deterministically even if the upstream proposer crashes completely, provided local sensing, braking authority, and stopping clearance remain intact. When those physical invariants hold, runtime filtering smoothly reconciles learned proposals with safety boundaries, preserving admissible task progress within the qualified physical envelope.

## The Minimal Intervention Principle and Optimization Filters {#sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention}

When the arm approaches the cage-door latch too quickly while still proposing a useful target and direction, rejecting every such proposal would discard useful learned behavior, whereas accepting it unchecked would exceed the permitted approach speed. The **minimal intervention principle**\index{Minimal intervention} resolves this trade-off by passing an admissible proposal untouched and choosing the smallest feasible correction—one that satisfies physical constraints and finishes before the permission deadline—whenever a proposal crosses a boundary. The resulting **safety shield**\index{Safety shield}\index{Minimal-intervention QP projection (safety shield)}[^fn-shield-safe-rl] preserves useful task progress within the physical limits. For the torque forbidden by @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque, the correction should remove only the constraint violation; replacing every near-boundary command with a stop would discard admissible learned behavior.

[^fn-shield-safe-rl]: **Shielding**: In safe reinforcement learning, a shield sits between the learning agent and its environment and overrides only those actions that would violate a temporal-logic safety specification [@alshiekh2018safe]. The CBF-QP is a continuous-control shield. Its override is the smallest torque change rather than a substituted discrete action, and its specification is a stopping margin rather than a logic formula, which lets it keep the learned action's direction instead of replacing it. \index{Shielding!safe reinforcement learning}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-cycle-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌── LOAD: declared enforcer cycle budget ────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

class EnforcementCycleBudget:
    scenario = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
    wcet = scenario.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared, not measured)
    deadline = scenario.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    tick = scenario.t_tick  # category: chosen
    unloaded = scenario.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative (unloaded observed cycle)
    acquisition = 30 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget; with the proposal check it covers the unloaded 40 us read in Ch13)
    proposal_lease = 15 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    tracking = 10 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    qp = 150 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    write = 15 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    reserve = 30 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    window = 500 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (rolling window of the intervention metric)

    # ┌── EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    total = (acquisition + proposal_lease + tracking + qp + write + reserve).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs((total - wcet.to(microsecond)).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The stage sub-budgets must sum to the declared WCET.")
    check(wcet < deadline < tick, "The declared WCET must sit inside the deadline, and the deadline inside the tick.")
    check(unloaded < wcet, "The unloaded observed cycle must sit below the declared WCET.")
    # margin_cbf_qp_cycle_budget_envelope.svg and its fig-alt hand-type 150, 250, 30, 400 and 135 us.
    check(
        [round(x.to(microsecond).magnitude) for x in (qp, wcet, reserve, deadline, unloaded)] == [150, 250, 30, 400, 135],
        "The cycle-budget margin figure's alt text states 150, 250, 30, 400 and 135 us.",
    )

    # ┌── OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    wcet_us_str = fmt(wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude, precision=0)
    deadline_us_str = fmt(deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude, precision=0)
    unloaded_us_str = fmt(unloaded.to(microsecond).magnitude, precision=0)
    acquisition_us_str = fmt(acquisition.magnitude, precision=0)
    proposal_lease_us_str = fmt(proposal_lease.magnitude, precision=0)
    tracking_us_str = fmt(tracking.magnitude, precision=0)
    qp_us_str = fmt(qp.magnitude, precision=0)
    write_us_str = fmt(write.magnitude, precision=0)
    reserve_us_str = fmt(reserve.magnitude, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rate_str = fmt_frequency((1 / tick).to("Hz"))
    window_ms_str = fmt_latency(window, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

For the already-derived torque half-space, the enforcer solves a constrained least-change problem, the **CBF-QP safety filter**\index{CBF-QP safety filter} [@ames2016control]. The tracker supplies the nominal effort; the barrier and actuator limits constrain the result. The combined program of @sec-appendix-control-clf, which optimizes convergence and safety together and relaxes convergence when they conflict, is not needed here. The tracker of @sec-enforcement-handoff already supplies the nominal effort, and the filter has only to keep it inside the barrier:
$$\min_{\ControlInput \in \mathbb{R}^\ControlInputDimension} \frac{1}{2}\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \BarrierConstraintNormal(\MechanicalPlantState)^\top \ControlInput \le \BarrierConstraintBound(\MechanicalPlantState), \quad \ActuatorTorqueLowerBound \le \ControlInput \le \ActuatorTorqueUpperBound$$ {#eq-enforce-cbf-qp}
where the half-space normal and threshold are defined by the directional derivatives $\BarrierConstraintNormal(\MechanicalPlantState)^\top = -\LieDerivativeAlongControl(\MechanicalPlantState)$ and $\BarrierConstraintBound(\MechanicalPlantState) = \LieDerivativeAlongDrift(\MechanicalPlantState) + \ClassKFunction(\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState))$ derived in @sec-enforcement-kinetic-barrier-certificates, matching the single-axis torque constraint of @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque, and $[\ActuatorTorqueLowerBound, \ActuatorTorqueUpperBound]$ represents the verified actuator torque envelope. The selected implementation allocates `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.qp_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ to this solve. Dedicated memory and a fixed iteration cap support that target; qualification must establish completion or a timely fallback under the admitted constraint set.

### Closed-form quadratic programming and torque projection {#sec-enforcement-qp-projection}

Clamping each joint axis independently, or projecting a command onto a barrier and then clipping it to motor torque limits afterward, can leave the coupled stopping constraint violated while skewing the direction of motion across task space. A single active barrier admits a closed-form projection when the projected command also lies inside the actuator bounds; if a bound becomes active, the enforcer must solve for the intersection rather than project onto the barrier and clamp afterward.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforce-cbf-qp-projection
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
import math
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class CBFQPProjection:
    u_nom = [3.5, 3.0]  # N·m; category: illustrative (abstract proposal)
    a_vec = [2.0, 1.0]  # category: illustrative (abstract half-space normal)
    b_scalar = 5.0  # N·m; category: illustrative (abstract threshold)
    u_clip = [2.0, 3.0]  # N·m; category: illustrative (per-axis clamp for contrast)
    u_lim = 5.0  # N·m; category: illustrative (symmetric per-joint actuator limit)

    res = calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection(u_nom, a_vec, b_scalar)
    u_proj = res["u_projected"]
    lambda_star = res["lambda_star"]
    correction_norm = res["correction_norm"]

    a_dot_u_nom = a_vec[0] * u_nom[0] + a_vec[1] * u_nom[1]
    breach = a_dot_u_nom - b_scalar
    a_dot_u_clip = a_vec[0] * u_clip[0] + a_vec[1] * u_clip[1]
    clip_penetration = a_dot_u_clip - b_scalar

    theta_nom_deg = math.degrees(math.atan2(u_nom[1], u_nom[0]))
    theta_clip_deg = math.degrees(math.atan2(u_clip[1], u_clip[0]))
    skew_deg = theta_clip_deg - theta_nom_deg

    check(abs(u_proj[0]) <= u_lim and abs(u_proj[1]) <= u_lim, "The projected command stays within the joint limits.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    u_nom_1_str = fmt(u_nom[0], precision=1)
    u_nom_2_str = fmt(u_nom[1], precision=0)
    a_1_str = fmt(a_vec[0], precision=0)
    a_2_str = fmt(a_vec[1], precision=0)
    b_str = fmt(b_scalar, precision=0)
    u_lim_str = fmt(u_lim, precision=0)

    a_dot_u_nom_str = fmt(a_dot_u_nom, precision=0)
    breach_str = fmt(breach, precision=0)
    lambda_star_str = fmt(lambda_star, precision=0)
    u_proj_1_str = fmt(u_proj[0], precision=1)
    u_proj_2_str = fmt(u_proj[1], precision=0)
    correction_norm_str = fmt(correction_norm, precision=3)

    u_clip_1_str = fmt(u_clip[0], precision=0)
    u_clip_2_str = fmt(u_clip[1], precision=0)
    a_dot_u_clip_str = fmt(a_dot_u_clip, precision=0)
    clip_penetration_str = fmt(clip_penetration, precision=0)
    theta_nom_deg_str = fmt(theta_nom_deg, precision=1)
    theta_clip_deg_str = fmt(theta_clip_deg, precision=1)
    skew_deg_str = fmt(skew_deg, precision=1)
```

For a nonzero constraint normal and inactive actuator bounds, the single barrier constraint $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput \le \BarrierConstraintBound$ in @eq-enforce-cbf-qp admits the closed-form projection derived in @sec-appendix-control-cbf-qp:
$$\CertifiedControlAction = \NominalControlCommand - \BarrierProjectionMultiplier^* \BarrierConstraintNormal, \qquad \BarrierProjectionMultiplier^* = \max\left(0, \frac{\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \NominalControlCommand - \BarrierConstraintBound}{\|\BarrierConstraintNormal\|^2}\right)$$ {#eq-enforce-cbf-projection}
where the optimal dual multiplier $\BarrierProjectionMultiplier^* \ge 0$ is zero whenever the nominal proposal is safe ($\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \NominalControlCommand \le \BarrierConstraintBound$), leaving $\CertifiedControlAction = \NominalControlCommand$. It is strictly positive when the proposal breaches the boundary ($\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \NominalControlCommand > \BarrierConstraintBound$). In that case it scales the minimal intervention vector $\FiniteChange \ControlInput = -\BarrierProjectionMultiplier^* \BarrierConstraintNormal$, which projects $\CertifiedControlAction$ orthogonally onto the safe half-space boundary $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput = \BarrierConstraintBound$.

On a two-axis manipulator with illustrative values, suppose the tracker following setpoints from an unconstrained neural policy computes nominal joint torques $\NominalControlCommand = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_nom_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_nom_2_str` $]^\top\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ against a validated safety half-space $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput \le \BarrierConstraintBound$. Its parameters are $\BarrierConstraintNormal = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_2_str` $]^\top$ and $\BarrierConstraintBound =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.b_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. The per-joint actuator limits are ±`{python} CBFQPProjection.u_lim_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Because the candidate gives $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \NominalControlCommand =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_dot_u_nom_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ and breaches the boundary by `{python} CBFQPProjection.breach_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, @eq-enforce-cbf-projection yields $\BarrierProjectionMultiplier^* =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.lambda_star_str` and projects the command to $\CertifiedControlAction = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_proj_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_proj_2_str` $]^\top\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. This meets the half-space exactly while keeping both joints within their limits at an intervention norm of `{python} CBFQPProjection.correction_norm_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. By contrast, an independent per-axis clamp that ignores the coupling and cuts only the joint with the larger normal component holds Joint 1 to `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_clip_1_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ while passing Joint 2 at `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_clip_2_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. That clamp gives $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ClampedControlCommand =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_dot_u_clip_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, still `{python} CBFQPProjection.clip_penetration_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ outside the constraint, while skewing the torque vector from `{python} CBFQPProjection.theta_nom_deg_str`$^\circ$ to `{python} CBFQPProjection.theta_clip_deg_str`$^\circ$. The per-axis clamp both violates the coupled constraint and distorts the command. Orthogonal projection satisfies the constraint with the smallest possible torque change, though it too rotates the torque vector, so the resulting end-effector path still requires checking against the coupled plant model.

This geometric behavior exposes the distinction between **torque-space and task-space minimal intervention**\index{Minimal intervention!torque vs. task space}: an orthogonal projection $\CertifiedControlAction = \NominalControlCommand + \FiniteChange \ControlInput$ minimizes joint effort deviation $\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2$, which redistributes multi-axis joint torques and rotates the net Cartesian wrench. While a feasible projection can preserve the safe set $\ForwardInvariantSafeSet$ under the stated model and timing assumptions, it deflects the end-effector trajectory and may arrest task progress. If the upstream neural policy continues emitting unprojected nominal setpoints without awareness of the intervention, the robot can chatter or stall at the boundary. The downstream enforcer must therefore stream the intervention vector $\FiniteChange \ControlInput$ back to the application processor as a telemetry signal, notifying the high-level planner to re-plan around the newly active physical constraint.

The same correction has a picture in state space and one in torque space (@fig-12-cbf-safety-filter). In state space, a trajectory that would breach the velocity-dependent boundary $\SafetyBoundaryManifold$ is turned along it; in the torque plane, the projection places $\CertifiedControlAction$ on the half-space boundary $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput = \BarrierConstraintBound$, while the per-axis clamp leaves $\ClampedControlCommand$ outside it and skews its direction.

::: {#fig-12-cbf-safety-filter fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Kinetic barrier and torque projection**: Panel (a) schematically shows a velocity-dependent viable boundary inset from geometric clearance; the raw distance alone has relative degree two for torque. Panel (b) illustrates Euclidean projection onto a supplied torque half-space. Panel (b) is schematic and not drawn to the worked example's values; that example's $[2,1]$ normal and $5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ threshold are abstract arithmetic inputs, not coefficients derived from the arm example." fig-alt="Two panels: a schematic inset stopping boundary in state space, and a two-axis torque plane in which a nominal command is projected onto a feasible half-space while a per-axis clamped command remains outside it."}
![](images/svg/fig12_cbf_safety_filter.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Filter choice joins a mathematical condition to a measured execution budget and the machine's available braking authority. As summarized in @tbl-12-safety-filter-architectures, architectural choices differ in their handling of relative degree, solver worst-case execution time (WCET), forward invariance guarantees, and directional fidelity. Independent clamping can miss coupled constraints; a CBF-QP can enforce a derived half-space if it is feasible and finishes within the verified cycle. Predictive filters [@wabersich2021predictive] trade a longer horizon for configuration-dependent compute cost.

The rows of @tbl-12-safety-filter-architectures belong to one unified family rather than rival techniques [@hsu2024safetyfilter]: each filter monitors a candidate against a **fallback policy**\index{Fallback policy!safety filter} known to keep the machine safe and intervenes whenever the candidate would leave the set from which that fallback still works, differing only in how the intervention occurs. Whereas a **least-restrictive**\index{Safety filter!least-restrictive} filter passes the proposal untouched up to the boundary and then switches abruptly to the fallback—which is simple to implement but chatters along the boundary—a smooth filter such as the CBF-QP blends in a correction before the boundary is reached. This chapter's enforcer combines both mechanisms: admitting a trajectory only with a matched stop suffix and holding a state-matched fallback for every reachable state forms a **backup-set filter**\index{Backup-set filter} that checks safety by rolling the fallback forward from the proposed state [@gurriet2018online; @chen2021backup]. The per-tick CBF-QP acts as the smooth local filter layered on top of it, and HJ reachability [@fisac2019general] supplies the value function when a precomputed surface replaces a closed-form barrier.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{26\baselineskip}
```

| Filter                         | Input and condition                                                                    | What it can establish                                                   | Main validation task                                                                                                          |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Independent torque clamp       | Each axis checked separately                                                           | Hardware amplitude limit, not coupled stopping clearance                | Test coupled wrench and stopping behavior                                                                                     |
| First-order CBF-QP             | Barrier whose first derivative contains the input                                      | Conditional invariance from a viable initial state                      | Validate model, feasible torque set, and cycle bound                                                                          |
| Kinetic / higher-order barrier | Position constraint with speed and braking authority included                          | Conditional stopping margin before geometric contact                    | Bound bias torque, delay, estimate error, and discretization                                                                  |
| Energy tank / passivity filter | State $\EnergyTankLevel$, power balance $\EnergyTankPower$, force $\ContactForceLimit$ | Conditional energy bound; force requires a separately qualified channel | Bound force-sensor bias, calibrate virtual damping matrix $\VirtualDampingMatrix$, and set reserve floor $\EnergyTankReserve$ |
| HJ value-function filter       | Precomputed value function over a gridded state space                                  | Containment for the modeled region                                      | Verify grid coverage, interpolation error, and disturbance bounds                                                             |
| Predictive safety filter       | Finite-horizon trajectory and terminal set                                             | Recursive feasibility only under terminal and timing assumptions        | Bound full solve time and fallback on timeout                                                                                 |

: **Safety-filter decisions**: A filter's physical claim depends on the chosen barrier and validated plant, not on the algorithm name. Nominal solve measurements are not worst-case deadlines. The energy-tank row is developed for intentional contact in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact. {#tbl-12-safety-filter-architectures tbl-colwidths="[20,26,28,26]"}

Operating near an active safe-set boundary can produce chattering. If a learned policy repeatedly proposes an unsafe command, sampled enforcement may switch the active constraint across successive `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` ticks. Depending on the plant and controller, rapid torque changes can excite a structural mode or increase motor heating and transmission wear. A tested boundary layer or hysteresis can reduce switching, but its added tracking error must fit inside the validated stopping margin.

The intervention vector $\FiniteChange \ControlInput = \CertifiedControlAction - \NominalControlCommand$ also measures upstream policy health. A rising intervention frequency or magnitude can indicate proposal drift, a changed task, or a changed plant. Normal filtering can also preserve successful whole-machine service while reducing unassisted proposer autonomy; the log must distinguish these outcomes rather than count every correction as a task failure. Summed over an illustrative rolling window of $\InterventionWindowDuration =$ `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.window_ms_str` as $\sum_{k} \|\CertifiedControlAction_k - {\NominalControlCommand}_k\| \FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, the metric lets the permission path flag divergence for logging or operator notification while the per-tick limits still protect the plant.

### Intentional contact and in-contact energy barriers {#sec-enforcement-intentional-contact}

Once the manipulator arm reaches the cage-door strike plate ($\AngularClearance = 0$), the spatial kinetic barrier (@eq-enforce-kinetic-barrier) reduces to $\BarrierFunction(0, \JointAngularSpeed) = -\JointAngularSpeed^2 / (2\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration) \ge 0$, which admits only zero speed ($\JointAngularSpeed = 0$) and freezes the gripper before it can depress the latch. A spatial kinetic barrier operates under the premise that the robot's objective is to avoid collision ($\AngularClearance > 0$), whereas manipulation, grasping, and assembly require intentional physical contact ($\AngularClearance = 0$). While the spatial barrier can admit arrival at contact with zero approach speed, it does not govern the subsequent force-controlled interaction where geometric separation no longer supplies the relevant margin. Once the warehouse mobile manipulator's gripper meets the strike plate at the guarded approach, the arm must push against the latch spring, and the margin that matters is the energy and force it delivers there.

Enforcing safety during intentional contact requires transitioning from a **spatial clearance barrier** to an **energetic passivity barrier**\index{Passivity observer!contact safety}\index{Energy tank!contact barrier function}. When physical clearance is zero ($\ClearDistance = 0$), safety cannot mean zero velocity; it means bounding mechanical energy exchange and normal contact force $\NormalContactForce$. A controller in physical contact interacts with an unmodeled, potentially stiff environment. If tracking errors or neural policy oscillations pump unmeasured energy into the interface, the closed-loop system undergoes contact chattering, limit cycles, or high-force impact spikes that damage both the workpiece and the robot's transmission.

To bound active energy exchange, the enforcer augments the controller state with an **energy tank** $\EnergyTankLevel(\TimeInstant)$[^fn-dissipativity-energy-tank] [@ferraguti2013tank; @hogan1985impedance] grounded in passivity. A passive system can return no more energy than its initial stored energy plus the energy it absorbs, so a power-preserving interconnection with a passive environment retains a passive energy balance (while a stability claim additionally requires the appropriate dissipation and state-observability conditions). The tank enforces that property by bookkeeping, acting as a software tally of work rather than a physical store of energy. Every joule that virtual damping removes from the arm's motion is credited to the tank, and the controller may spend actively only what the tank holds, namely its accumulated credits plus a fixed initial reserve. In this contact formulation, $\ActiveControlTorque$ denotes the active torque component excluding damping, so the total controller torque is $\ActiveControlTorque-\VirtualDampingMatrix\GeneralizedVelocities$. The damping term can credit the tank only to the extent that the actuator actually realizes the corresponding dissipative work, and using total torque in the debit while also crediting damping would count the same dissipation twice. With those components separated, the modeled balance is:
$$\EnergyTankPower = \GeneralizedVelocities^\top \VirtualDampingMatrix\,\GeneralizedVelocities - \ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities$$ {#eq-enforce-energy-tank}
where $\GeneralizedVelocities^\top \VirtualDampingMatrix\,\GeneralizedVelocities \ge 0$ is the dissipative power credited under qualified torque tracking and $\ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities$ is active mechanical power. Saturation, delay, or tracking error requires conservative bounds on realized work rather than credit for an unrealized damping request. The enforcer then defines the energy-tank barrier certificate of @eq-enforce-energy-cbf:
$$\EnergyTankBarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState, \EnergyTankLevel) = \EnergyTankLevel - \EnergyTankReserve \ge 0$$ {#eq-enforce-energy-cbf}
where $\EnergyTankReserve > 0$ is a reserved baseline. Combined with a hard contact-force limit $\ContactForceBarrierFunction(\MeasuredContactForce) = \ContactForceLimit - \|\MeasuredContactForce\| \ge 0$, the enforcer establishes the in-contact viable set $\InContactViableSet$. While $\EnergyTankLevel > \EnergyTankReserve$ and $\|\MeasuredContactForce\| < \ContactForceLimit$, candidate neural actions are admitted to perform manipulation. If the task consumes the allocated energy budget ($\EnergyTankLevel \to \EnergyTankReserve$) or contact force approaches $\ContactForceLimit$, the barrier filter clamps active energy injection ($\ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities \le 0$), restricting active work under the modeled power balance. This energy constraint does not by itself bound contact force, because a passive interaction with a stiff surface can still produce a large force. The force channel needs its own sensing-error, response-delay, and actuator bounds before the combined constraints can justify continued contact.

[^fn-dissipativity-energy-tank]: **Dissipativity**: @willems1972dissipative generalized circuit passivity to any dynamical system with a storage function, an energy-like quantity that can grow no faster than the power supplied to the system. Interconnected passive systems inherit that bound, which is why contact with an unknown but passive environment can be kept stable without a model of the environment. The energy tank is a storage function that the controller keeps explicitly in software, so the bound holds only as far as the tank's bookkeeping matches the work the actuators actually do. \index{Dissipativity!energy tank}

For a contact command, integrating the work balance in @eq-enforce-energy-tank over one control interval $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ supplies the energy allowance for the same least-change decision. Suppose the current tank level is ${\EnergyTankLevel}_0\ge \EnergyTankReserve$, a conservative lower bound on damping power actually realized is $\RealizedDampingPower$, and a bounded contact-direction speed $\ContactDirectionSpeed>0$ is held over this simplified interval. The spendable work is then ${\EnergyTankLevel}_0-\EnergyTankReserve+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$. Because a proposed constant force $\ProposedContactForce \ge 0$ debits $\ProposedContactForce \ContactDirectionSpeed \FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, the energy allowance caps force at $\EnergyLimitedContactForce=({\EnergyTankLevel}_0-\EnergyTankReserve+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)/(\ContactDirectionSpeed\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)$. Letting $\ContactForceCap$ denote the smaller of the deliverable force and the contact-force ceiling after sensing and delay allowances, the admitted command under these stipulated scalar conditions is $\AdmittedContactForce = \min(\ProposedContactForce, \EnergyLimitedContactForce, \ContactForceCap)$, whose debit leaves ${\EnergyTankLevel}_1={\EnergyTankLevel}_0+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant-\AdmittedContactForce \ContactDirectionSpeed\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\ge \EnergyTankReserve$ while keeping force below the independent cap. The controller can therefore continue useful contact with a reduced force instead of abandoning the task. At the reserve with no credited damping, however, no positive active work is admitted. Zero speed requires a separate force check rather than division by speed, and delayed or uncertain power requires conservative work bounds over the interval.

The force channel's own bounds can be computed for the running machine's two contacts: the cage door, which the arm pushes on purpose, and the coworker's hand, which it must never press too hard. Each calculation turns a force limit into a speed that the enforcement record carries as a channel ceiling, and each rests on premises that only a measurement can settle. They are derived here, where the channel is enforced; the release decision consumes the results as premises.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Contact force and speed ceilings are enforced as release premises in @sec-release-question.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-contact-force
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONTACT FORCE AT THE DOOR AND AT THE HANDOVER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact (latch and handover paragraphs,
# │          @eq-release-trip-indentation, @eq-release-coupled-indentation,
# │          @eq-release-unbraked-force), @fig-10-latch-force-budget.
# │ Goal:    derive once, where the channel is enforced, the latch force at
# │          brake onset and the stop it requires, and the handover contact
# │          force and speed ceilings; release cites these as premises.
# │ Show:    latch force-rise rate, force at onset, remaining compression, arm
# │          deceleration and stop time at the guarded and unsupported
# │          approaches; hand-arm reduced mass, transient force at the TCP limit
# │          and at the handover speed, clamped force, both speed ceilings.
# │ How:     calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile (AISLE latch fields);
# │          calc_reduced_mass, calc_transient_impact_force,
# │          calc_transient_contact_speed_limit with the ISO/TS 15066 hand body
# │          model (AISLE.m_contact_human, AISLE.k_contact_human).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_reduced_mass,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_transient_contact_speed_limit,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_force_rate,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementContactForce:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (guarded approach)
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    k_latch = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative
    t_contact = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (contact loop)
    f_lim = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived
    m_hand = AISLE.m_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    k_hand = AISLE.k_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    f_contact = AISLE.f_contact_criterion  # category: chosen
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen (handover approach under accept_item)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen (free-space TCP limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stop_lo = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch, scenario=AISLE)
    stop_hi = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch_high, scenario=AISLE)
    df_dt = stop_lo["df_dt"]
    f_cmd = stop_lo["f_at_brake_onset"]
    x_rem = stop_lo["x_remaining"]
    a_arm = stop_lo["a_arm_needed"]
    t_arm_stop = stop_lo["t_arm_stop"]
    f_cmd_hi = stop_hi["f_at_brake_onset"]
    a_arm_hi = stop_hi["a_arm_needed"]
    m_red = calc_reduced_mass(m_eff, m_hand).to(kilogram)
    f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(tcp_limit, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / f_contact).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_handover_clamped = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand).to(newton)
    v_ceiling = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling_clamped = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand).to(meter / second)
    # Notebook operands: sqrt(k_H * mu) for the free and the clamped hand (N per m/s)
    imp_free = ((k_hand * m_red) ** 0.5).to(newton / (meter / second))
    imp_clamped = ((k_hand * m_eff) ** 0.5).to(newton / (meter / second))
    clamp_ratio = (imp_clamped / imp_free).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, guarded approach, is 39 N.")
    check(abs(x_rem.to(millimeter).magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Remaining latch compression is 0.15 mm.")
    check(abs(a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "The guarded stop needs about 3 m/s^2 (2.95).")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "The guarded stop takes about 10 ms.")
    check(abs(f_cmd_hi.to(newton).magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, unsupported approach, is 95 N.")
    check(abs(a_arm_hi.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "The unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2.")
    check(f_cmd < f_lim and f_cmd_hi < f_lim, "Both approaches reach brake onset below the latch limit.")
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Arm effective contact mass is 12.0 kg.")
    check(abs(m_red.magnitude - 0.5714) < 5e-5, "Hand-arm reduced mass is 0.571 kg.")
    check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit is 207 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N.")
    check(f_handover < f_contact < f_handover_clamped, "Transient passes and clamped fails the criterion.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Free-hand ceiling is 0.24 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand ceiling is 0.053 m/s.")
    check(v_ceiling_clamped < v_handover < v_ceiling, "The handover cap sits between the clamped and free-hand ceilings.")
    check(abs((v_handover * imp_free).to(newton).magnitude - f_handover.magnitude) < 1e-9, "Notebook: v * sqrt(k mu) reproduces the free-hand force.")
    check(
        abs((f_contact / imp_clamped).to(meter / second).magnitude - v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "Notebook: F_h / sqrt(k m_eff) reproduces the clamped ceiling.",
    )
    check(4.0 < clamp_ratio < 5.0, "Clamping multiplies the force by between four and five.")
    # margin_handover_clamp_force_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 20.7 N, 94.9 N and the 50 N criterion.
    check(abs(f_contact.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "The handover force criterion is 50 N.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    k_latch_str = fmt_sci_qty(k_latch, newton / meter, precision=1)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(t_contact, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    df_dt_nms_str = fmt_force_rate(df_dt, unit=newton / millisecond, precision=0)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd, precision=0)
    f_cmd_high_str = fmt_force(f_cmd_hi, precision=0)
    f_lim_str = fmt_force(f_lim, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_rem.to(millimeter).magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_arm_high_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_hi, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(round(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m_hand_str = fmt_mass(m_hand, unit=kilogram, precision=1)
    k_hand_str = fmt_stiffness(k_hand, unit=newton / millimeter, precision=0)
    m_red_str = fmt_mass(m_red, unit=kilogram, precision=2)
    tcp_limit_str = fmt_velocity(tcp_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(f_contact, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    f_handover_clamped_str = fmt_force(f_handover_clamped, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    k_hand_nm_str = fmt(k_hand.to(newton / meter).magnitude, precision=0, commas=True)
    m_red_val_str = fmt(m_red.magnitude, precision=3)
    m_eff_val_str = fmt(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude, precision=0)
    m_hand_val_str = fmt(m_hand.to(kilogram).magnitude, precision=1)
    v_handover_val_str = fmt(v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude, precision=2)
    f_contact_val_str = fmt(f_contact.to(newton).magnitude, precision=0)
    imp_free_str = fmt_int(round(imp_free.magnitude))
    imp_clamped_str = fmt_int(round(imp_clamped.magnitude))
    clamp_ratio_str = fmt(clamp_ratio, precision=1)
```

At the door the quantity that matters is how fast force rises. Against a strike plate of stiffness $\LatchPlateStiffness$, an arm approaching at $\LatchApproachSpeed$ raises the contact force at $d\NormalContactForce/d\TimeInstant = \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed$, which at the guarded `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_latch_str` against the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.k_latch_str` plate is `{python} EnforcementContactForce.df_dt_nms_str`. The contact tripwire fires at $\ContactTripwireForce =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_trip_str`, but the contact loop needs $\ContactLoopResponseTime =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.t_contact_str` for detection, command delivery, and torque rise, and the plate keeps compressing by $\LatchApproachSpeed \ContactLoopResponseTime$ before deceleration begins. The force at physical braking onset is therefore
$$\BrakingOnsetContactForce = \ContactTripwireForce + \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed\,\ContactLoopResponseTime$$ {#eq-release-trip-indentation}
which evaluates to `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_str`, well inside the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_lim_str` latch limit. The limit still binds the stop that follows, because the plate goes on compressing while the arm sheds its remaining kinetic energy:
$$\MaximumPlateIndentation = \frac{\BrakingOnsetContactForce}{\LatchPlateStiffness} + \frac{\LatchApproachSpeed^2}{2\ArmStoppingDeceleration} \le \frac{\LatchForceLimit}{\LatchPlateStiffness}$$ {#eq-release-coupled-indentation}
Against time since first contact (@fig-10-latch-force-budget), force climbs through the tripwire and across the loop-response window to `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_str` at brake onset; the commanded stop then bends the curve over to finish at the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_lim_str` latch limit, while an unbraked run crosses the limit within a few milliseconds. The braking term ignores the plate's spring work, which would help decelerate the arm, so the bound is conservative. Below the limit the plate can compress only `{python} EnforcementContactForce.x_remaining_str` further, and stopping within that distance requires about `{python} EnforcementContactForce.a_arm_str`, an illustrative stop of about `{python} EnforcementContactForce.t_arm_stop_str`.

::: {#fig-10-latch-force-budget fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Latch contact force against time**: Force on the strike plate rises at `{python} EnforcementContactForce.df_dt_nms_str` from first contact. It crosses the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_trip_str` tripwire, but the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.t_contact_str` contact-loop response lets it reach `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_str` before the brake command. A stop at about `{python} EnforcementContactForce.a_arm_str`, lasting about `{python} EnforcementContactForce.t_arm_stop_str`, brings the arm to rest exactly at the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_lim_str` limit; without the brake, force crosses the limit within a few milliseconds. The plate is modeled as a linear spring and the arm as rigid." fig-alt="Plot of contact force in newtons against time since first contact in milliseconds. A solid line rises straight from zero, passes a dotted tripwire line at 15 newtons, crosses a shaded band labeled response 2 milliseconds, and reaches a dot labeled brake command 39 newtons. After the dot the line bends over and levels off exactly at a dashed limit line labeled latch limit 100 newtons, with a label reading arm stop about 3 meters per second squared, about 10 milliseconds. A dashed red line labeled no brake continues straight up from the dot and crosses the limit near 8 milliseconds. The region above the limit is shaded."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-latch-force-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LATCH CONTACT FORCE AGAINST TIME (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-latch-force-budget
# │
# │ Goal:    show why the stop must be sized from the force already reached at
# │          brake command, not from the tripwire.
# │ Show:    rise at k*v to the 15 N tripwire, 2 ms response to 39 N, the sized
# │          arm stop peaking at the 100 N limit; the unbraked rise for contrast.
# │ How:     reads calc-enforcement-contact-force (EnforcementContactForce);
# │          guards that the drawn profile hits 39 N at command and 100 N at rest.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, newton, meter, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check

# ┌── 1. LOAD (values from calc-enforcement-contact-force) ────────────────────
K = EnforcementContactForce.k_latch.to(newton / meter).magnitude  # N/m
V = EnforcementContactForce.v_latch.to(meter / second).magnitude  # m/s
F_TRIP = EnforcementContactForce.f_trip.to(newton).magnitude
F_LIM = EnforcementContactForce.f_lim.to(newton).magnitude
T_RESP = EnforcementContactForce.t_contact.to(second).magnitude
F_CMD = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude
A_ARM = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude
T_STOP = EnforcementContactForce.t_arm_stop.to(second).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: force from first contact through the arm stop ──────────────
t_trip = F_TRIP / (K * V)
t_cmd = t_trip + T_RESP
tau = np.linspace(0.0, T_STOP, 200)
f_brake = F_CMD + K * (V * tau - 0.5 * A_ARM * tau**2)
t_rise = np.linspace(0.0, t_cmd, 50)
f_rise = K * V * t_rise
check(abs(f_rise[-1] - F_CMD) < 1e-6, "latch figure: rise reaches the brake-command force")
check(abs(f_brake[-1] - F_LIM) < 1e-6, "latch figure: the sized stop peaks exactly at the latch limit")
ms = 1000.0
t_end = (t_cmd + T_STOP) * ms
t_nb = np.linspace(t_cmd, t_end, 50)
f_nb = K * V * t_nb / ms

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
viz.set_book_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.grid(False)
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
Y_TOP = 1.45 * F_LIM
ax.axhspan(F_LIM, Y_TOP, color=R["consequence"], alpha=0.07, lw=0)
ax.axhline(F_LIM, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))
ax.text(t_end * 1.02, F_LIM + 3, f"latch limit {F_LIM:.0f} N", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["consequence"])
ax.axhline(F_TRIP, color=R["neutral"], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 2)))
ax.text(t_end * 1.02, F_TRIP + 2, f"tripwire {F_TRIP:.0f} N", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"])
```
