```{python}
ax.axvspan(t_trip * ms, t_cmd * ms, color="#D97706", alpha=0.14, lw=0)
ax.text((t_trip + t_cmd) / 2 * ms, Y_TOP * 0.93, f"response\n{T_RESP * ms:.0f} ms", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9, color="#B45309")
ax.plot(t_nb, f_nb, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (5, 3)), clip_on=True)
ax.text(t_nb[18], min(f_nb[18], Y_TOP) + 2, "no brake", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["consequence"])
ax.plot(t_rise * ms, f_rise, color=R["structural"], lw=2.0)
ax.plot((t_cmd + tau) * ms, f_brake, color=R["structural"], lw=2.0)
ax.plot([t_cmd * ms], [F_CMD], "o", ms=5, color=R["structural"])
ax.annotate(
    f"brake command {F_CMD:.0f} N",
    xy=(t_cmd * ms, F_CMD),
    xytext=(t_cmd * ms + 1.0, F_CMD - 16),
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["structural"],
    va="top",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=R["structural"], lw=0.7),
)
ax.text(
    (t_cmd + 0.58 * T_STOP) * ms,
    F_CMD + 22,
    f"arm stop ≈ {A_ARM:.0f} m/s², ≈ {T_STOP * ms:.0f} ms",
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["structural"],
)
ax.set_xlim(0, t_end * 1.03)
ax.set_ylim(0, Y_TOP)
ax.set_xlabel("time since first contact (ms)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("contact force (N)", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The same two equations show why the approach speed is an enforced channel rather than a preference. At the chunk policy's proposed `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_latch_high_str` (@sec-enforcement-authority-refuse), @eq-release-trip-indentation already gives `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_high_str` at braking onset, and @eq-release-coupled-indentation then demands an arm deceleration of `{python} EnforcementContactForce.a_arm_high_str`. The faster approach spends the response interval on force that the stop can no longer absorb. This is the physical half of the refusal in @sec-enforcement-authority-refuse; the evidential half is that no trial sampled this speed. Both results treat the arm as rigid and the plate as the whole contact stiffness. Gripper, wrist-sensor, and joint compliance in series lower the effective stiffness and slow the rise, while a geared joint reflects rotor inertia into the moving mass. Whether this arm achieves the required deceleration within a fraction of a millimeter depends on joint torque, drive rise time, and structural stiffness that only arm stopping trials establish. A compliant element placed in series on purpose turns that softening into passive protection. Springs in series add their compliances, so the combined stiffness falls below that of the softer element and the force rises more slowly, a protection that holds even when the enforcer cannot stop in time. The stiffness of that element is therefore part of the contact margin, and @sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment sizes it for this latch.

The coworker's hand is the opposite case, a contact the task tolerates only up to a bounded peak force. The force depends first on which contact occurs. In a *transient* contact the hand is free and recoils, so both bodies move and the collision acts through their reduced mass $\ReducedImpactMass$. In a *clamped* (quasi-static) contact the hand is trapped against a rack upright or the robot's own body, cannot recoil, and receives the full robot-side effective mass at the tool center point, $\EffectiveImpactMass =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_eff_str`. The biomechanical body model of ISO/TS 15066:2016, whose collaborative-application requirements ISO 10218-2:2025 now incorporates (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions), assigns the hand and fingers an effective mass $\BodyRegionMass$ of `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_hand_str` and an effective spring constant $\HertzianContactStiffness$ of `{python} EnforcementContactForce.k_hand_str` [@isots15066; @iso10218part2; @kirschner2022iso15066]. This worked example estimates the robot-side mass as half the arm's moving mass plus its payload capacity; it does not compute the configuration- and direction-dependent mass reflected through the contact Jacobian. In an unbraked elastic contact the peak force is
$$\UnbrakedImpactForce = \ContactApproachSpeed\,\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\,\ReducedImpactMass}, \qquad \ReducedImpactMass = \left(\frac{1}{\BodyRegionMass} + \frac{1}{\EffectiveImpactMass}\right)^{-1}$$ {#eq-release-unbraked-force}
This is the spring-mass bound of @eq-training-impact-peak, which equated a moving mass's kinetic energy to the peak elastic energy of the contact, with one change: two bodies move. Momentum conservation keeps the pair's common (center-of-mass) motion unchanged through the contact, so only the kinetic energy of their relative motion, $\frac{1}{2}\ReducedImpactMass \ContactApproachSpeed^2$ for a closing speed $\ContactApproachSpeed$, can compress the hand, and the reduced mass takes the place of the single moving mass. For this hand and arm, $\ReducedImpactMass$ is `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_red_str`, because the light hand dominates the sum; a clamped hand is the limit $\BodyRegionMass \to \infty$, in which $\ReducedImpactMass$ becomes $\EffectiveImpactMass$. Solved for speed at a force criterion $\HandForceCriterion$, the equation gives the channel ceiling $\ContactApproachSpeed = \HandForceCriterion/\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\,\ReducedImpactMass}$. The peak follows the assumed masses and stiffness; the model establishes neither an impact duration nor a pressure or injury limit.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The single-mass spring-impact bound that this reduced-mass form extends is established in @sec-training-contact-exploit.
:::

At the arm's `{python} EnforcementContactForce.tcp_limit_str` free-space limit even the transient model predicts `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_tcp_str`, or `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_ratio_mult_str` the `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_contact_str` criterion, so the arm cannot enter an unseparated contact at that speed. At the handover speed the two contact cases bound the approach very differently (notebook \ref{nbk-enforcement-clamped-hand-penalty}).

::: {#nbk-enforcement-clamped-hand-penalty .callout-notebook title="The clamped-hand penalty"}

**Problem**: The arm approaches the coworker's hand at the handover speed. What peak force does @eq-release-unbraked-force predict for a free hand that recoils and for a hand clamped against a rack upright, and what approach speed does the force criterion allow in each case?

**Variables**:

* $\EffectiveImpactMass =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_eff_str` (Derived; the simplified half-arm-mass plus payload-capacity estimate used above).
* $\BodyRegionMass =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_hand_str` and $\HertzianContactStiffness =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.k_hand_str` (Datasheet; the ISO/TS 15066 hand body model).
* $\ContactApproachSpeed =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_handover_str` (Chosen; the handover approach while the coworker holds the `accept_item` grant that @sec-intervention-human-authority defines).
* $\HandForceCriterion =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_contact_str` (Chosen; the handover force criterion).

**Math**: For a free hand, $\ReducedImpactMass =$ (1/`{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_hand_val_str` + 1/`{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_eff_val_str`)$^{-1} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.m_red_val_str` kg, and with $\HertzianContactStiffness =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.k_hand_nm_str` N/m the stiffness term is $\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_free_str` N per m/s. The peak force is $\ContactApproachSpeed\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_handover_val_str` $\times$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_free_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_str`, and the criterion admits $\HandForceCriterion/\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_contact_val_str` $/$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_free_str`, or `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_str`. A clamped hand cannot recoil, so $\ReducedImpactMass$ becomes $\EffectiveImpactMass$ and $\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness \EffectiveImpactMass} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_clamped_str` N per m/s. The same approach then delivers `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_handover_val_str` $\times$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_clamped_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_clamped_str`, and the criterion admits only `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_contact_val_str` $/$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.imp_clamped_str`, or `{python} EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped_str`.

**Result**: The free hand sees `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_str`, inside the criterion; the clamped hand sees `{python} EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_clamped_str`, which fails it.

**Systems insight**: Clamping multiplies the force at any speed by $\sqrt{\EffectiveImpactMass/\ReducedImpactMass} =$ `{python} EnforcementContactForce.clamp_ratio_str`, because the whole arm-side mass, not the light hand, sets the collision. A speed ceiling derived for a free hand is therefore a geometric premise as much as a kinematic one.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_handover_clamp_force_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars of peak contact force at the handover speed: a free hand at 20.7 newtons, below a red dashed line at the 50 newton criterion, and a clamped hand at 94.9 newtons, in red, past it."}

*At one handover speed a free hand passes the force criterion and a clamped hand fails it.*
:::

The handover channel is therefore a transient-contact ceiling. It holds only while the handover geometry excludes clamping, with the handover point in free space and no rack upright, tote edge, or link of the arm within reach of the hand along the approach. Both contacts end the same way. The arithmetic is exact; what it cannot supply is the premise it rests on, whether an achievable arm deceleration, a contact stiffness, or a clamp-free geometry. The enforcement record keeps each ceiling beside that premise, and the same discipline governs every barrier in this chapter.

### The conditions forward invariance rests on {#sec-enforcement-invariance-conditions}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-zoh-buffer
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTER-SAMPLE DRIFT UNDER ZERO-ORDER HOLD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the discretization condition below and the ZOH fallacy.
# │ Goal:    size the inter-sample buffer v T + a T^2 / 2 on the base.
# │ Show:    drive limit, independent approach-acceleration upper bound, buffer.
# │ How:     RM.base.max_velocity, stipulated approach upper bound, AISLE.t_tick.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementZOHBuffer:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_max = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_approach_upper = (
        2.0 * meter / second**2
    )  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (independent approach-acceleration upper bound, not credited braking)
    t_ctrl = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_zoh = (v_max * t_ctrl + 0.5 * a_approach_upper * t_ctrl**2).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_zoh.magnitude - 1.501) < 1e-9, "The ZOH buffer at the drive limit is 1.501 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v_max, precision=1)
    a_str = fmt_acceleration(a_approach_upper, precision=0)
    dzoh_str = fmt_length(d_zoh, unit=millimeter, precision=3)
```

Unmodeled friction loss, actuator saturation, solver overruns, or inter-sample drift under a held torque command can each push a physical plant across a barrier boundary even when the continuous-time inequality is satisfied at the sample instant. The containment claim provided by both spatial and energetic barrier calculations is therefore strictly conditional. A forward-invariance claim requires a feasible barrier and the following bounded conditions; the list is necessary for this design, not an exhaustive if-and-only-if test:

1. **Model Fidelity:** The nominal plant dynamics $\ControlAffineDriftField(\MechanicalPlantState)$ and $\ControlAffineInputField(\MechanicalPlantState)$ must capture the true system dynamics within a validated parameter error bound.
2. **Disturbance Bounds:** External forces and unmodeled friction acting on the mass must remain strictly within the modeled disturbance envelope $|\ExternalDisturbanceForce(\TimeInstant)| \le \DisturbanceForceBound$.
3. **Actuation Authority:** Physical actuators must possess sufficient voltage, current, and thermal headroom to realize the commanded corrective force within a qualified delivered-effort error and response-delay envelope, as well as without saturation ($\ActuatorEffort^* \in [\MinimumActuatorEffort, \MaximumActuatorEffort]$).
4. **Solver Determinism:** The optimization solver or projection algorithm must terminate strictly within its allocated execution budget ($\FilterSolveTime \le \FilterSolveBudget < \PermissionLoopPeriod$).
5. **Discretization Invariance:** The discrete sampling interval $\PermissionLoopPeriod$ must be sufficiently small that inter-sample state drift does not breach the continuous-time invariance boundary.

The approach-acceleration upper bound is a separate premise from the lower bound on available braking, and equality of their illustrative magnitudes does not identify their roles. Each of the five conditions maps to a dedicated engineering budget: model fidelity and disturbance bounds come from system identification and bench load testing, actuation authority from dynamometer curves and thermal limits, solver determinism from static worst-case execution time analysis on the MCU, and discretization from the loop period itself. Because the drive holds the last admitted command between samples (a zero-order hold[^fn-zoh-hold-drift]), the plant drifts for one full period before the next check can act on it. The drift covers at most $\FiniteChange \ZohHoldTravel = \BodySpeed \PermissionLoopPeriod + \frac{1}{2} \ProfileAccelerationBound \PermissionLoopPeriod^2$ at speed $\BodySpeed$, where the worst case is the highest speed the base can reach rather than the ceiling $\SpeedBound$ that admission enforces. At the `{python} EnforcementZOHBuffer.v_str` drive limit, an independently stipulated `{python} EnforcementZOHBuffer.a_str` upper bound on approach acceleration, and $\PermissionLoopPeriod =$ `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str`, that drift is `{python} EnforcementZOHBuffer.dzoh_str`, a small fraction of $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin$. Tightening a raw-clearance check by this displacement preserves geometric separation over the hold interval under the stated motion bounds, whereas a kinetic or energy barrier requires a bound on its own evolution throughout the interval.

[^fn-zoh-hold-drift]: **Zero-Order Hold**: The order counts the derivatives the hold carries forward. A zero-order hold keeps the command's value constant until the next sample, while a first-order hold would also extrapolate its slope. For one control tick the plant therefore integrates a torque the controller can no longer change, which is the source of the drift buffer $\BodySpeed \PermissionLoopPeriod + \frac{1}{2}\ProfileAccelerationBound \PermissionLoopPeriod^2$; @sec-appendix-control-zoh develops the hold's delay. \index{Zero-order hold!inter-sample drift}

A condition that no detector watches is an assumption, so the permission path attaches one to each. A **disturbance observer**\index{Disturbance observer} compares predicted with measured acceleration on every cycle. Inverter status registers and current shunts report actuator saturation\index{Actuator saturation}. A hardware watchdog\index{Hardware watchdog} and cycle counter time the solver against its deadline. Timestamp counters on the sensor bus catch jitter and missed samples. When a detector invalidates a premise, the enforcer cannot restore permission by substituting optimistic parameters. It selects a response whose sensing, effort, and clearance premises survive, as developed in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. Both the free-space projection and contact decision must finish before the physical margin reserved for computation is spent.

### Execution timing in the sub-millisecond loop {#sec-enforcement-loop-budget}

A correct barrier calculation delivered after the permission deadline cannot protect the margin reserved for that deadline. The whole cycle must therefore have a bounded execution time [@wilhelm2008worst], including state acquisition and the final drive transfer. A real-time operating system can reduce scheduling delays, but its name does not establish a bound on shared-memory or peripheral interference. The permission path's implementation must be qualified under the competing workloads that can delay it, so the declared cycle allocation below is a timing requirement carried into loaded placement tests rather than a measured trace or a platform-independent solver guarantee.

In this heterogeneous design, the shield executes inside a `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.rate_str` timer interrupt routine on the MCU. An unloaded cycle of acquisition, validation, and a typical active-set solve completes in about `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.unloaded_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$, an illustrative estimate rather than a bound. The candidate path instead declares a worst-case execution-time requirement of `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.wcet_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ for the whole cycle, divided among the stages below, and the whole sequence must finish inside the `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.deadline_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ deadline:

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_cbf_qp_cycle_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal bar of the 250 microsecond declared WCET, split into the QP solve at 150 in orange, the other stages in dark slate, and the 30 microsecond reserve in light slate, with empty headroom out to a red dashed line at the 400 microsecond deadline. A small tick below the bar marks the unloaded run at 135."}

*The QP solve takes `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.qp_us_str` of the `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.wcet_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ declared cycle, inside a `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.deadline_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ deadline.*
:::

1. **Interrupt Entry & State Acquisition (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.acquisition_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** The hardware timer triggers the interrupt service routine (ISR), and firmware latches the wheel and joint encoder registers and the latest inertial measurement unit (IMU) sample.
2. **Proposal & Lease Verification (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.proposal_lease_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** The MCU makes one bounded read of its local mailbox, which the link receiver fills outside this routine, validates the checksum, and confirms sequence order before checking evidence age, the active chunk lease, and the host heartbeat timer. In the evidence-age check, the evidence's age at dispatch is the difference between the source frame's evidence timestamp and the host dispatch timestamp in the proposal header (@sec-nervous-supervisory-timers). That age may not exceed `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.age_threshold_str`, which combines the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.t_age_str` observation age charged in row 5 of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget with `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.eps_sync_str` of clock uncertainty (@sec-perception-observation-contract). Passing that test qualifies the evidence only at dispatch, so the MCU also reconstructs the evidence's current age from its source epoch and elapsed time and checks it against the evidence's own validity deadline and the remaining physical margin. Inference, admission, waiting, and transfer after dispatch must already be reserved once in that margin through the dispatch-to-admission allocation inside the timing allowance. Otherwise fresh evidence is required before activation, because a new proposal timestamp cannot renew old evidence. The MCU then verifies that elapsed time since valid admission or renewal has not exceeded the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.lease_ms_str` active chunk lease and reads the host heartbeat timer, which marks the host silent once no heartbeat has arrived within the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_timeout_ms_str` timeout.
3. **Tracking Contract Verification (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.tracking_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** Firmware evaluates instantaneous tracking error norm $\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\| = \|\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant) - \ReferencePosition(\TimeInstant)\|$ against the qualified bound $\TrackingErrorBound$.
4. **CBF-QP Safety Shield Solve (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.qp_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** An active-set QP solver[^fn-activeset-qp-dual] running in pre-allocated static SRAM, the MCU's tightly coupled data memory, evaluates active barrier inequalities and computes $\CertifiedControlAction = \arg\min_{\ControlInput \in \mathbb{R}^\ControlInputDimension} \frac{1}{2}\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2$. A fixed iteration cap limits the work count; meeting the allocation also requires bounded per-iteration arithmetic, memory access, interrupt interference, and output service, including ill-conditioned constraint geometry. Dynamic memory allocation is forbidden on this path so that heap service is excluded from that timing obligation. In this two-processor design no memory is shared with the host, so camera direct memory access (DMA) streams cannot reach the memory this cycle uses. The couplings that remain are the link receiver, whose DMA writes into the MCU's own memory, and any shared supply rail or clock; @sec-placement-hardware-allocation measures that residual interference and tests whether the isolation holds under load.
5. **Output Selection & Admitted Command Staging (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.write_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** If the QP is feasible and constraints hold, the enforcer emits the **admitted command**\index{Admitted command!enforcement record}. The drives close the velocity and current loops. Because industrial servo drives running in position mode choose torque direction internally from position tracking error while an unsigned torque limit clips only the magnitude of each joint's effort symmetrically, a position setpoint plus an unsigned torque limit does not by itself realize the signed braking effort or coupled multi-axis half-space the QP requires. This interface needs a qualified mapping from the staged command to delivered effort, with bounded realization error and response delay. The filter tightens each commanded half-space by the largest possible projection of that effort error along its normal, so every effort the drive may realize still satisfies the delivered-effort constraint. Near full braking, that allowance may remove feasibility and require earlier intervention. The drive configuration and qualification evidence must establish these bounds; this example supplies no measured error or delay. During the response interval, a previously held command must remain valid and the intersample/response allowance must cover its effect, charging each delay once. If the position/limit interface cannot satisfy this contract, the design needs a qualified effort interface or a stricter qualified operating envelope and fallback. The next position setpoint and per-axis torque limit travel in the next EtherCAT frame only under that realization contract. Drive-reported torque on the following tick can detect a breach but cannot retroactively certify the preceding interval; an invalid replacement leaves previously admitted setpoints in force only while their own evidence, lease, state, and stopping reservation remain valid.
6. **Completion & Reserve (`{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.reserve_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$):** The MCU checks the register write and services its own watchdog only after the cycle succeeds. The reserve absorbs variation in the stages above; a cycle that has not completed by the deadline requires a qualified preempting timer or an independent mechanism to select the resident fallback before the next tick. The overrunning ISR cannot be assumed to detect and recover from its own stall. Only with that bounded transfer does a missed tick cost the base `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.missed_tick_str` of travel at the aisle speed. @Sec-placement-testing-separation tests whether the declared WCET holds under load, so that ticks are not missed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The schedulability analysis that a declared WCET and deadline feed is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-timers.
:::

[^fn-activeset-qp-dual]: **Active-Set QP**: An active-set solver guesses which constraints hold with equality, solves the resulting linear system, and adds or drops one constraint per iteration. Dual variants such as that of @goldfarb1983numerically start from the unconstrained optimum, here the nominal command itself, and add only violated constraints, so a proposal that already satisfies every barrier costs almost nothing. The iteration count is bounded by the combinations of the constraint set rather than by a clock, so a fixed iteration cap bounds steps while the time per step must still be measured under interference. \index{Quadratic programming!active-set method}

Stage 5 is also where refusal takes effect. Any of several conditions triggers it. The chunk lease may have expired, the host heartbeat may have fallen silent, the shared drive bus may report undervoltage, tracking error $\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\|$ may exceed $\TrackingErrorBound$, actuator saturation may render the feasible control set empty ($\SafeControlSet = \emptyset$), or an operating-contract detector such as the disturbance observer or the solver deadline may trip. In any of these cases, the output selector withholds the admitted command, revokes policy authority, and selects the state-matched stop. At standstill, lease or heartbeat expiry selects HOLD, the powered standstill hold that @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder defines, only while powered support remains available. Undervoltage instead requires a qualified transition to mechanical restraint before that support expires. In motion, STOP under undervoltage remains conditional on drive survival.

::: {#chk-enforcement-barrier-filter-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Barrier, projection, and cycle budget"}

The barrier fixes which commands preserve the stop; the filter and its cycle decide whether the chosen command arrives in time.

- [ ] **Relative degree**: Why does a barrier on raw distance give torque no control authority at the boundary, and what does the kinetic barrier of @eq-enforce-kinetic-barrier add to restore it?
- [ ] **Projection vs. clamp**: Why can clamping each joint separately leave a coupled half-space violated, while @eq-enforce-cbf-projection satisfies it with the smallest torque change?
- [ ] **Projection estimate**: Treat the latch approach as a one-dimensional speed command whose half-space is the `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_str` target-ODD ceiling. What are $\BarrierProjectionMultiplier^*$ and the admitted speed when the chunk policy proposes `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_high_str`?
- [ ] **Timing premise**: Which of the five forward-invariance conditions do the declared `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.wcet_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ WCET and the `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.deadline_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ deadline defend, and what must select the fallback when a cycle overruns?

:::

Every stage of this cycle assumes that the solve returns a feasible command. When saturation empties the admissible torque set, the lease lapses, or the cycle overruns its deadline, projection has nothing to return, and the permission path must already hold a response it can execute without the proposer. Executing that check deterministically while surviving proposer faults requires placing the enforcer where the host processor cannot preempt or bypass it.

## Admission, Cyclic Checking, and Monitor Independence {#sec-enforcement-where-enforcer-sits}

A planned waypoint can clear a warehouse rack upright in the planner's geometric check while the physical manipulator overshoots into the steel during execution, and an instantaneous motor torque well within electrical limits can accelerate the arm past the point where its remaining stopping reservation can arrest motion. Relying on trajectory admission alone misses in-flight tracking overshoot and saturation, whereas checking only single-step torque commands without a verified stopping continuation lets the arm enter an inevitable collision state before the local filter reacts. Robust safety enforcement therefore demands both layers (the per-tick cycle of @sec-enforcement-loop-budget on a dedicated MCU and full-plan admission before motion begins). That raises three structural questions: why neither layer can replace the other, where the cyclic checker sits relative to the command stream, and how independent of the proposer the MCU must actually be.

Full-plan admission judges the candidate trajectory, its seams, its swept clearance, and its verified stopping continuation before the machine commits to motion. The expensive geometry behind that judgment (queries of global occupancy octrees, signed distance fields, or mesh collision models) cannot run inside a `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` control interrupt merely because the MCU owns final actuation privilege. It therefore runs on the host as a separately scheduled, bounded job, and its result reaches the MCU as the trajectory record. The MCU's own admission check then verifies that record against bounded, qualified local evidence (the resident stop suffix, its entry state, and the commitment deadline) without traversing the global map. The hard real-time cyclic path evaluates current joint state, remaining lease validity, and available actuator effort on every tick before selecting and dispatching the next physical command.

An in-line checker places its worst-case execution time directly inside the control-loop deadline, consuming a portion of the available compute tick. A parallel monitor instead operates asynchronously alongside the proposal pipeline, avoiding added forward latency during nominal execution but contributing detection latency and trip delay to the physical response budget. Either architectural placement must ensure privilege isolation. The untrusted proposer must never be able to bypass the selected output, and the system must preserve the dedicated sensing and actuation channels required by the fallback controller. As @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die will show from the resources each candidate placement shares, isolating these execution domains across memory spaces or heterogeneous processing cores is what allows the safety monitor and its fallback mechanisms to survive the very proposer faults that trigger an intervention. The physical stopping budget supplies the non-negotiable temporal and spatial boundaries that this hardware split must satisfy.

::: {#psp-enforcement-simplex-independence .callout-perspective title="The monitor independence rule"}
Any valid safety claim must explicitly define which proposer failure modes its sensing, compute, and actuation pathways survive. Placing a monitor on a separate physical core or processor does not establish true independence if that monitor shares a power rail, a memory bus, a sensor link, or an unisolated clock domain with the untrusted proposer. Shared hardware resources require provably bounded interference or a qualified, survivable fallback state. Any environmental condition that the monitor cannot observe directly must remain an explicit, documented operating premise rather than an unstated assumption.
:::

The running example assumes qualified drive, scanner, and arm safety functions and a rated lease/heartbeat watchdog; the release case must name the scoped evidence supporting those functions. Independence, however, is not certification. The runtime permission path is not the machine's certified functional safety layer, and beneath it sit the certified safety functions embedded within motor drives, safety laser scanners, and the dedicated safety controller. These hardware-interlocked mechanisms carry the formal integrity claims that certification bodies audit against industrial standards. The primary operational duty of the software permission path is to regulate the learned proposer proactively so that the robot never trips those certified hardware interlocks during normal operation. @Sec-enforcement-certified-functions maps each dynamic response developed throughout this chapter onto that underlying certified safety floor once the complete response hierarchy is established, and names the one narrow MCU function that does carry a rating.

### Where the thesis bends {#sec-enforcement-thesis-bends}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-torque-policy
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A LEARNED POLICY AS THE CONTROL-RATE CONTROLLER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the "where the thesis bends" paragraphs immediately below.
# │ Goal:    price what the lease row of the stopping budget becomes when the
# │          policy itself emits a command every tick.
# │ Show:    lease-path travel at the aisle speed for the chunk lease and for a
# │          per-tick command stream.
# │ How:     AISLE lease, tick, and bus fields (rows 4 of the stopping budget).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementTorquePolicy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_row = (v_aisle * (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus)).to(millimeter)
    tick_row = (v_aisle * (t_tick + t_bus)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(lease_row.magnitude - 80.6) < 1e-6, "The chunk-lease row is 80.6 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs(tick_row.magnitude - 2.6) < 1e-6, "A per-tick command stream leaves 2.6 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_row_str = fmt_length(lease_row, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    tick_row_str = fmt_length(tick_row, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

When a learned locomotion or manipulation policy emits raw joint targets or motor torques at the control rate instead of handing the permission path a multi-step trajectory, the enforcer loses the ability to verify a collision-free stopping continuation before motion begins. It must then either run an active fallback model on every tick or watch its projections induce distributional shift and boundary chattering. Admission and the cyclic check in this chapter both assume that the proposer hands the permission path a plan it can judge before motion: kinematic intent lives in the learned policy, and deterministic motor drives close the torque loops. Much of contemporary robot learning practice abandons this classical division, outputting joint targets at the control rate above stiff proportional-derivative loops [@lee2020learning] or emitting motor torques end-to-end. The third law, proposal is not permission (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}), does not disappear in such direct control designs. Instead, the range of physical guarantees that the runtime permission path can uphold narrows in precise, quantifiable ways.

Four guarantees survive because each acts directly on raw commands at the causal boundary, without requiring a forward plan. A per-tick limit on rate and amplitude bounds torque slew and joint velocity at the hardware register interface. The kinetic barrier of @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque operates directly in effort space, so a CBF-QP can filter the policy's output without converting it to an intermediate kinematic setpoint. The passivity-based energy tank of @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact monitors power exchange and bounds the physical work the policy can inject into the environment during contact. Beneath all of these, low-level geofencing, safely-limited speed monitoring, and torque removal backed by mechanical spring brakes remain permanently active under the software stack. Communication timing improves along one dimension. If a qualified freshness deadline is selected at one tick and an independent watchdog enforces it, policy silence is detected within that tick plus bus transport delay, which reduces the lease-expiration travel row of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget from `{python} EnforcementTorquePolicy.lease_row_str` to `{python} EnforcementTorquePolicy.tick_row_str` at the aisle speed.

What is lost is admission. Without an explicit multi-step trajectory, the system cannot verify the collision-free stopping suffix before the robot commits to motion. The enforcer must instead evaluate the machine's dynamic stopping reservation on every tick against an active fallback controller that maintains its own internal braking model. On a wheeled mobile base, that fallback is straightforward to formulate. The controller executes a qualified service-braking response along the current heading, followed by wheel restraint after confirmed standstill. On an underactuated balancing machine, such as a bipedal humanoid, the fallback is itself an active balance controller; cutting motor torque produces an immediate uncontrolled fall rather than a safe state.

Runtime projection also alters the closed sensorimotor loop under which the policy was trained. Every time the enforcer projects a proposed action onto the admissible set, it delivers a state to the environment that the policy never intended, precipitating distributional shift in subsequent observations. This penalty surfaces directly in task performance, as quantified by the intervention metrics of @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention. Frequent overrides cause the machine to chatter erratically along safety boundaries or freeze conservatively short of its goal. To reconcile this tension, modern architectures adopt filter-aware policy training, incorporating the safety filter directly into the training objective so that the neural network learns to avoid the boundary rather than encountering the enforcer for the first time on physical hardware [@hsu2024safetyfilter]. The core thesis still holds at the causal boundary, where untrusted proposals never bypass runtime enforcement. What bends is how much of the safety argument can be settled mathematically before motion begins vs. how much performance the machine must sacrifice to settle the remainder while moving.

## The Fallback Ladder {#sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder}

A safety filter must select its fallback before the admissible control set becomes empty. Once the chosen filter has an empty feasible intersection, it cannot maintain its modeled invariant. A qualified alternate response may mitigate damage or support its own narrower containment claim, but selecting it does not restore the lost guarantee. Furthermore, physical systems cannot rely on a single, binary kill switch. Abruptly severing DC bus power whenever a control proposal approaches a barrier boundary induces uncontrolled deceleration, mechanical shock, and incessant false-positive mission aborts. Conversely, complex software optimization is futile during a hardware fault such as an inverter shoot-through, because the fault destroys gate-driver field-effect transistors (FETs) milliseconds before an interrupt handler can even dispatch.

To resolve these competing physical realities, the permission path maintains a deterministic ladder of resident protective responses. The runtime arbiter evaluates plant kinematics, remaining sensor validity, and hardware integrity on every control cycle, selecting deterministically among minimally invasive projection, closed-loop position holding, controlled deceleration, or complete torque removal. The name records an ordering by how much control authority each response retains, from a corrected proposal down to unpowered restraint, not a sequence to descend. The arbiter never climbs down the rungs one at a time; it jumps directly to the one whose prerequisites still hold.

::: {#dfn-enforcement-dynamic-fallback-ladder .callout-definition title="Dynamic fallback ladder"}

***Dynamic fallback ladder***\index{Fallback ladder!definition}\index{Dynamic fallback ladder|see{Fallback ladder}} is the set of resident protective responses ($\ControlInput \in \{\SafeSetProjection(\NominalControlCommand), \PoweredHoldCommand, \ControlledStopCommand, \TorqueCutoffCommand\}$). A deterministic arbiter selects one of them on every tick according to the check that failed (an invariant violation, a timing overrun, or a hardware fault) and the measured state of the plant. One trigger can therefore select different rungs in motion and at standstill.

1.  **Significance**: Physical AI systems cannot treat all faults identically. Cutting actuator power on dynamic, underactuated, or high-momentum plants (for example, legged robots mid-stride or multirotors in flight) precipitates immediate catastrophic falls or tumbling. These platforms require state-matched active deceleration before executing terminal torque removal.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike software exception handlers that unwind the call stack or terminate a user-space thread, a dynamic fallback ladder operates against physical momentum. The arbiter matches each rung to the remaining valid sensor channels, surviving control authority, and available stopping clearance.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the rungs as an escalation sequence where lower rungs, such as safe torque off (STO), inherently provide faster or safer arrest. Each rung possesses distinct entry prerequisites; invoking an unpowered torque inhibit on an airborne drone or an unbraked mobile base allows the machine to coast freely without arresting motion.

:::

### The four rungs of the fallback ladder {#sec-enforcement-four-rungs}

Walking down protective responses one step at a time like a software exception cascade fails on physical hardware: commanding a standstill position hold while the base is rolling at `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` saturates the drives, while cutting drive torque before active braking completes lets the vehicle coast into the obstacle. The dynamic fallback architecture therefore organizes protection across four resident responses (`PROJECT`, `HOLD`, `STOP`, and `INHIBIT`). The deterministic arbiter samples measured plant state (velocity, position, payload loading) and fault severity on every millisecond tick to dispatch the response whose compute, sensing, and actuation prerequisites still hold:

1. `PROJECT`, minimal-intervention projection in MCU firmware. The primary safety filter executes on every control cycle while the feasible control set is nonempty ($\SafeControlSet \neq \emptyset$), the proposal lease is fresh, and tracking error remains within bounds ($\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\| \le \TrackingErrorBound$). It computes the minimal-intervention torque $\CertifiedControlAction = \arg\min_{\ControlInput} \|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2$ subject to active barrier half-spaces within its `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.qp_us_str` $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ cycle allocation. It makes the smallest feasible effort correction under the stated invariance assumptions; the planner must still account for any changed task-space path.
2. `HOLD`, powered hold at standstill in MCU firmware. When the machine is stationary, the arbiter selects an energized position hold, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 2 stop: safe stop 2 (SS2) followed by safe operating stop (SOS), the drive function that monitors standstill.[^fn-stop-category-iec60204] Its protective validity stems from that certified standstill monitor rather than the position loop gain. Because IEC 60204-1 permits only Category 0 or Category 1 for an emergency stop, HOLD can never serve as an E-stop response [@iec60204]. The drives maintain coordinate $\PoweredHoldState$ under closed-loop position control, modulating inverter phase currents against gravity and static loads. While this rung incurs continuous Joule heating in motor windings\index{Joule heating}, it eliminates friction brake wear and preserves kinematic calibration, enabling instantaneous task resumption when a valid trajectory proposal arrives. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, this rung handles lapsed leases or lost host heartbeats specifically when the platform is already at standstill.
3. `STOP`, controlled dynamic stop in MCU firmware. When a machine in active transit loses proposal authority, tracking error diverges, or an obstacle breaches the stopping envelope, the response is a resident, state-matched controlled stop, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop (safe stop 1, SS1). Its certified counterpart is the ramp-monitored variant (SS1-r), which checks deceleration against a bounded profile throughout the arrest; the unmonitored, time-controlled variant (SS1-t) merely removes torque after a fixed delay without verifying that the planned ramp actually decelerated the load [@iec61800part52]. The resident jerk-limited S-curve stop suffix of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes serves this role provided the entry state falls within its validated domain. Executed autonomously by bare-metal MCU firmware directly from local SRAM, this stop peaks at the credible deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$, returning kinetic energy through motor inverters to the DC bus for absorption by the qualified regeneration path. Power removal and mechanical brake clamping occur only after confirmed zero velocity.
4. `INHIBIT`, torque inhibit and spring-brake clamping by hardware interlocks. When the safety microcontroller suffers a brownout, clock loss, or watchdog timeout, all software decision logic ceases. Dedicated, out-of-band hardware interlocks trigger STO to de-energize gate drive power supplies and drop hold current to electromechanical spring-applied brakes. This terminal rung removes motor torque without software intervention; the mechanical brakes provide only their independently qualified holding or dynamic stopping capacity.

[^fn-stop-category-iec60204]: **Machine Stop Categories**\index{IEC 60204-1!Stopping categories}\index{Functional safety!Emergency stop categories}: IEC 60204-1 distinguishes uncontrolled power removal (Category 0), controlled stopping followed by power removal (Category 1), and controlled stopping with power retained (Category 2). A category defines electrical power status rather than stopping distance; every rung therefore requires its own empirically validated stopping measurement.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-stop-rung
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE STOP RUNG ON THE MACHINE'S BASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the controlled-stop paragraph immediately below.
# │ Goal:    show that the stop rung executes the resident C2 suffix.
# │ Show:    aisle speed, credible deceleration, suffix duration and distance.
# │ How:     calc_scurve_stop_time / _distance on AISLE.v_aisle and
# │          AISLE.a_brake; jerk bound from calc_c2_stop_suffix at the drive limit.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance, calc_scurve_stop_time
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementStopRung:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # reference polynomial's peak jerk
    duration = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    distance = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(duration.magnitude - 931.25) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s takes 931.25 ms.")
    check(abs(distance.magnitude - 605.3125) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s covers 605.31 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    duration_str = fmt_latency(duration, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    distance_str = fmt_length(distance, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
```

When a machine in motion loses proposal authority or violates a tracking bound, the arbiter engages a controlled dynamic stop, operating analogously to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop\index{Safe stop 1}. On the warehouse mobile manipulator base, this rung executes the resident stop suffix pre-admitted alongside the motion trajectory, rather than attempting to synthesize a stopping trajectory on the fly during a fault. In steady-state cruising with zero acceleration, this pre-computed profile matches the operating state at fault onset directly; nonzero acceleration states require their own qualified state-matched suffixes. From an aisle cruise velocity of `{python} EnforcementStopRung.v_aisle_str`, the jerk-limited S-curve suffix sustains a credible peak deceleration of `{python} EnforcementStopRung.a_brake_str` between its jerk transitions. The entire maneuver spans `{python} EnforcementStopRung.duration_str` and traverses `{python} EnforcementStopRung.distance_str`, the stop-suffix travel the stopping budget of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes reserves at this speed. Because the deceleration phase channels kinetic energy back through the inverter into the DC bus, bus capacitance and braking choppers must absorb this regenerative surge without triggering a bus overvoltage fault. Complete electrical power removal, if mandated by protocol, occurs only after sensors verify standstill.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-rail-holdup
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL AND THE UNBUDGETED INHIBIT RUNG
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the inhibit paragraph immediately below.
# │ Goal:    compare logic/coil hold-up with the selected stop sequence;
# │          inverter torque survival is a separate qualification premise.
# │ Show:    spring-brake engage range, hold-up, flag-to-brakes-set time, margin.
# │ How:     RM D15 rail fields; the S-curve suffix at the inspected-floor
# │          ceiling (EnforcementStoppingBudget) with the friction-bound peak
# │          and the load's jerk bound.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_time
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementRailHoldup:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen
    engage_min = RM.spring_brake_engage_min  # category: illustrative
    engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    a_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_inspected  # category: derived (mu_inspected_floor * g)
    v_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_inspected  # category: derived (inspected-floor ceiling)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    flag_to_onset = (tick + bus + onset).to(millisecond)
    longest_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_inspected, a_inspected, EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake).to(millisecond)
    flag_to_set = (flag_to_onset + longest_stop + engage_max).to(millisecond)
    margin = (holdup - flag_to_set).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "The permission rail holds up for 2.0 s.")
    check(abs(flag_to_onset.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Stop onset follows the flag within 22 ms.")
    check(abs(flag_to_set.magnitude - 1313.43) < 5e-3, "Flag to all brakes set is 1313.43 ms.")
    check(abs(margin.magnitude - 686.57) < 5e-3, "The hold-up leaves 686.57 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    engage_min_ms_str = fmt_latency(engage_min, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    engage_max_ms_str = fmt_latency(engage_max, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    holdup_str = fmt_latency(holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
    flag_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    longest_stop_str = fmt_latency(longest_stop, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    flag_to_set_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_set, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    margin_str = fmt_latency(margin, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
```

Beyond firmware-driven stops, a separate out-of-band circuit can inhibit motor torque generation entirely. Drive STO cuts gate-drive bias to isolate inverter FETs, but it does not disconnect the DC bus, energize mechanical friction brakes, or actively decelerate a moving rotor; an unbraked motor will simply coast under its existing momentum. In robust architectures, an external safety controller simultaneously drives a separately rated contactor and spring-applied mechanical brakes. Engineers must evaluate the dynamic stopping distance of this combined pathway as an integrated system, because dropping drive torque while an arm is under gravitational load or while a vehicle is at speed can exacerbate the hazard. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, this pathway, STO combined with nine spring brakes that engage between `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_min_ms_str` and `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_max_ms_str` after coil flux decay, constitutes the unbudgeted INHIBIT rung. It serves exclusively as a hardware backstop for MCU cycle failure, and the primary stopping envelope claims do not rely on it.

An undervoltage fault on the shared drive bus can invoke the STOP rung only while inverter gate drives, angular encoders, and control logic retain adequate voltage for closed-loop deceleration. The isolated permission rail maintains power to logic circuits, transceivers, and brake coils for `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.holdup_str`, but it does not supply the motor currents required for braking torque. Consequently, timing guarantees for powered stopping assume a surviving drive bus. Under this condition, dynamic braking begins within `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.flag_to_onset_str` of the fault flag; the hold-up hypothetical uses the pre-dispatch inspected-floor ceiling of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_inspected_str`, rather than an admitted operating configuration, and its stop requires `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.longest_stop_str`. Mechanical brake engagement at standstill adds at most `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_max_ms_str`. This entire sequence completes within `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.flag_to_set_str`, preserving a `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.margin_str` buffer of control logic hold-up.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The isolated permission rail and its capacitive hold-up are established in @sec-body-permission-rail-isolation.
:::

This analysis confirms the control-supply duration budget, whereas the electrical drive-energy budget requires separate qualification. Systems engineers must prove through empirical testing that the DC bus capacitance, inverter power stages, and regenerative dump resistors sustain controlled deceleration under worst-case electrical fault conditions. If the drive stage cannot guarantee this power integrity, the system must either adopt an unpowered dynamic braking configuration or restrict its operational safety envelope; INHIBIT cannot be credited with standard Category 1 stopping performance. Similarly, at standstill, an undervoltage fault must trigger verified mechanical brake engagement before the logic supply decays, rather than attempting to maintain an active HOLD indefinitely on finite capacitance.

Physical AI systems engineers must distinguish between **fail-safe** and **fail-operational** plants when configuring terminal fallbacks. In a machine already at a mechanically restrained standstill, removing drive torque is safe once mechanical engagement is verified. On underactuated, open-loop unstable, or high-momentum platforms, however, abruptly removing actuator torque directly initiates a catastrophic failure mode:

1. **Aerial platforms (multirotors and eVTOLs)**: Cutting motor torque drops aerodynamic thrust to zero instantly, transforming an airborne vehicle into an uncontrolled ballistic projectile.
2. **Dynamic legged systems (bipedal humanoids)**: During dynamic locomotion, the robot's center of mass frequently falls outside the support polygon; stability depends on active ground-reaction forces and momentum exchange. Suddenly removing joint torques causes an unrecoverable fall, with impact severity governed by gait phase and available compliance.
3. **High-speed autonomous vehicles**: De-energizing steering actuators or electric traction motors at highway speeds strips away the control authority required to execute a coordinated deceleration, leaving the vehicle at the mercy of passive road friction.

The physical channel that dispatches a hardware torque-removal request is the out-of-band interlock that @sec-nervous-actuation-authority traced (@fig-real-estop). In it, dual linked emergency-stop contacts, two force-guided relays whose external device monitoring (EDM) contacts block a restart after a weld, and two STO inputs on the drive leave no single fault able to defeat the trip. What the INHIBIT rung needs from that circuit is its third stage, drawn again here with the brake in its own loop (@fig-12-estop-interlock), because removing drive torque ($\CommandedJointTorque = 0$) and arresting physical momentum are distinct functions that need separate validation:

1.  **Torque removal (Stage 3, drive side):** De-energizing the safety relays drops the drive's STO inputs, which de-energize the gate drive power supply for the three-phase inverter bridge, rendering the power MOSFETs or insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) high-impedance, so the motor can no longer produce electromagnetic torque. STO alone does not apply mechanical braking. An unbraked motor carries momentum and may coast freely.
2.  **Mechanical restraint (Stage 3, brake side):** A separate coil circuit powers the spring-applied electromechanical friction brake. When power is removed, coil magnetic flux decays, allowing internal springs to physically clamp friction pads against the motor shaft, applying the brake without electrical power. A holding-brake rating does not establish the ability to arrest a moving load; dynamic stopping requires separate energy, torque, and response qualification.

::: {#fig-12-estop-interlock fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative emergency-stop circuit**: Stages 1 and 2 are the out-of-band interlock circuit (Chapter 4); Stage 3 maps to the numbered list above. Two linked contacts each hold a force-guided relay, the relays' enable contacts hold the drive's two Safe Torque Off (STO) inputs, and their EDM contacts in series block a restart after a weld. The spring-applied brake runs on its own supply, and a supply contactor, if fitted, provides galvanic disconnection. A moving motor can coast after STO, so the brake's set time and the physical stopping distance must be measured for the load and state." fig-alt="Two-channel schematic in three labeled stages. Stage 1, dual-channel E-stop: a red positive-break E-stop mechanically linked to normally closed contacts S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. Stage 2, redundant relays with EDM: S1 drives the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact, and the EDM contacts in series run with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. Stage 3, separate stop functions: K1 and K2 send STO1 and STO2 enable to the drive, whose gate-drive supply feeds an inverter bridge driving motor M, tagged in red tau equals 0 and noted may coast. A dashed box above the drive reads supply contactor, if fitted. A brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft, with a dashed tag reading brake set time: measure."}
![](images/svg/fig12_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

That separation between software control and hardwired, out-of-band trip circuits is not a stylistic preference. When the processor running the control loop stalls or corrupts its own state, only a physically independent path can still remove drive enable and clamp the brakes. The precedent that the lineage table of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws attaches to the third law shows the cost of removing that hardware path and trusting software logic to gate a high-energy actuator on its own (war story \ref{ws-enforcement-therac-25-software-interlock-elimination}).

::: {#ws-enforcement-therac-25-software-interlock-elimination .callout-war-story title="Therac-25 software interlock elimination"}
**Context**: Between 1985 and 1987, the Therac-25 medical linear accelerator administered massive radiation overdoses to six cancer patients after system designers eliminated the electromechanical interlocks used in previous models, assigning safety-critical beam containment entirely to software [@leveson1993investigating].

**Mechanism**: Software race conditions and shared memory corruption in the operator interface allowed the machine to fire its high-current electron beam (25 MeV) without rotating the tungsten target and beam-flattening filter into position. Because the physical microswitches that previously interlocked beam activation had been removed, the underlying hardware possessed no independent means to detect that the operational mode conflicted with the turntable state.

**Impact**: Six patients received radiation doses estimated between 4,000 and 20,000 rads (up to 100 times the therapeutic level), causing severe tissue necrosis and three direct fatalities [@leveson1993investigating].

**Response**: Investigators mandated the restoration of independent hardware interlocks, requiring positive electromechanical verification of turntable configuration prior to beam generation, alongside formal software safety lifecycle standards.

**Systems lesson**: A software-based protection layer cannot serve as its own independent backstop. A runtime barrier filter may exercise binding authority over nominal control proposals, but the architecture still requires an out-of-band, physically independent trip mechanism to survive processor lockups, memory corruption, and firmware bugs. Moreover, because torque removal alone does not guarantee deceleration, the surviving physical response must match the plant's dynamic envelope.
:::

The four rungs run on two paths (@fig-12-fallback-ladder). `PROJECT`, `HOLD`, and `STOP` run in safety MCU firmware at the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.loop_rate_str` tick and reach the drives through one arbiter, which selects a single actuation command $\SelectedActuationCommand$; `INHIBIT` bypasses the firmware on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply (STO) and drops spring-brake holding current when the processor itself fails. The rungs trade response latency, control authority, and recovery cost, and the arbiter selects directly among those whose entry prerequisites still hold. A controlled stop demands verified drive electronics and sufficient stopping clearance; losing drive integrity forces unpowered mitigation with strictly weaker physical guarantees. Selection is also only as sound as the state evidence behind it. The 2023 Cruise pullover, which @sec-boundary-when-fails set beside Tempe as a failure after impact, selected a motion fallback on the strength of a missing track (war story \ref{ws-enforcement-cruise-fallback-dragging}).

::: {#fig-12-fallback-ladder fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Fallback responses and the paths that run them**: The plant state and the failed check select one response directly; the four are alternatives, not steps of an escalation. PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in the safety MCU's firmware and reach the drives through its arbiter, which here passes the projected command. INHIBIT is the one response that survives loss of the MCU itself, so it bypasses the arbiter on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply and lets the spring brakes set. On a moving machine that path also removes motor braking, and the machine coasts until the separately qualified brakes take hold." fig-alt="Four rows, each with a condition card on the left joined by an arrow to a response card. The first three responses, PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP, sit inside a dashed box labeled safety MCU firmware, 1 kHz, and feed a multiplexer whose selected input, PROJECT, connects to an output arrow labeled u act entering a tall box labeled drives and brakes. The fourth response, INHIBIT, sits in a separate dashed box labeled hardware interlock and connects directly to the drives box by an arrow labeled STO, brake supply. The PROJECT condition, proposal u nom admitted, is drawn dashed in bronze."}
![](images/svg/fig12_canonical_fallback_ladder.svg){width="100%"}
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-incident-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TEMPE AND CRUISE RECORDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the Cruise war story below, the Tempe pitfall, and
# │          @fig-12-uber-tempe-timeline.
# │ Goal:    print the investigators' values instead of hand-typed literals.
# │ Show:    Tempe first detection 5.6 s and recognition 1.2 s before impact;
# │          Cruise pullover about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up to 7.7 mph (3.4 m/s).
# │ How:     literature values from NTSB/HAR-19/03 and the Quinn Emanuel
# │          report, the same values as @sec-boundary-when-fails loads, kept
# │          here until the literature registry holds them.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

class EnforcementIncidentRecord:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019), p. v and table pp. 15-16
    t_detect = 5.6 * second  # first detection, before impact
    t_recognize = 1.2 * second  # imminent collision recognized, before impact
    # category: literature. Quinn Emanuel report to the Cruise boards (2024), p. 10
    d_drag = 20 * foot  # approximate distance moved during the pullover
    v_drag = 7.7 * mph  # maximum speed during the pullover

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_drag_m = d_drag.to(meter)
    v_drag_ms = v_drag.to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_recognize < t_detect, "Recognition comes after first detection.")
    # fig-12-uber-tempe-timeline fig-alt hand-types 5.6 s and 1.2 s.
    check(abs(t_detect.magnitude - 5.6) < 1e-9 and abs(t_recognize.magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "The NTSB times are 5.6 s and 1.2 s.")
    check(abs(d_drag_m.magnitude - 6.096) < 1e-3, "20 ft is 6.1 m.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_recognize_str = fmt_latency(t_recognize, unit=second, precision=1)
    d_drag_str = fmt_length(d_drag, unit=foot, precision=0)
    d_drag_m_str = fmt_length(d_drag_m, unit=meter, precision=1)
    v_drag_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag, unit=mph, precision=1)
    v_drag_ms_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag_ms, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

::: {#ws-enforcement-cruise-fallback-dragging .callout-war-story title="Cruise post-impact fallback (2023)"}
**Context**: In October 2023, an autonomous Cruise robotaxi in San Francisco encountered a pedestrian who had been struck by an adjacent human-driven vehicle and propelled into the robotaxi's travel lane [@exponent2024cruise].

**Mechanism**: The autonomous vehicle initiated an immediate emergency stop upon detecting the impact. However, the collision-classification subsystem erroneously localized the pedestrian to the side of the vehicle rather than under the chassis, categorizing the event as a side collision. The operational design domain for side collisions specified a secondary pullover maneuver to clear traffic. Because the perception pipeline had tracked the pedestrian only intermittently before the collision, the tracker marked the lane ahead as clear, prompting the vehicle to accelerate from standstill into the pullover [@exponent2024cruise].

**Impact**: Executing the pullover dragged the pedestrian, who remained pinned beneath the vehicle's floorpan, approximately `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.d_drag_str` (`{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.d_drag_m_str`) at speeds reaching `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.v_drag_str` (`{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.v_drag_ms_str`), causing severe trauma [@quinnemanuel2024cruise]. The California DMV subsequently suspended Cruise's autonomous testing and deployment permits, prompting Cruise to halt fleet operations nationwide and recall software across 950 vehicles [@cadmv2023cruise; @exponent2024cruise].

**Response**: A post-collision fallback must prohibit renewed motion whenever state uncertainty persists. In this scenario, retaining a locked standstill and mandating physical inspection prevents the system from treating missing perceptual tracks as free space. Teleoperation feeds cannot substitute for verified local sensor coverage.

**Systems lesson**: An embodied fallback cannot infer free space from the absence of sensor tracks. Every transition across fallback states requires positive evidence verifying that assumed physical invariants hold, paired with failsafe physical restraints while state ambiguity remains unresolved.
:::

### Industrial stop categories and the safe torque off trap {#sec-enforcement-stop-categories}

On a moving mobile base or a gravity-loaded arm, Safe Torque Off (STO) is not an active brake: removing drive torque immediately leaves the base coasting on wheel momentum and lets the arm drop during the milliseconds before its mechanical friction brakes clamp. Decelerating the mobile manipulator safely instead uses closed-loop motor torque during the active braking phase and engages mechanical holding brakes only once the plant reaches confirmed standstill. Industrial standards distinguish machine-level stop categories from drive-level safety functions across this sequence. IEC 60204-1 classifies whether electrical power remains connected during and after deceleration. Functional safety standards such as IEC 61800-5-2 define the drive functions, including STO, SS1, and SS2, that execute individual stages of a response, and the `HOLD` and `STOP` rungs borrowed their names from them. @Tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories maps these formal classifications to their concrete physical obligations.

| Response                                                    | Motor torque and power                                                         | Physical stop obligation                                                                           | Appropriate use                                          |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Admitted filtering                                          | Drive remains active                                                           | Recheck the feasible kinetic barrier and tracking bound every tick                                 | Nominal operation inside the validated envelope          |
| Controlled hold (Category 2 / SS2-like)                     | Power remains for braking and hold                                             | Verify stopping distance, thermal headroom, and static load support                                | Hold when feedback and torque authority remain available |
| Controlled stop then torque removal (Category 1 / SS1-like) | Power remains through deceleration; torque is removed afterward                | Verify the full braking and transition time under load                                             | Moving machine with enough reserved clearance            |
| Torque removal (Category 0 / STO-like)                      | Drive cannot produce commanded torque; DC bus isolation is a separate function | A moving motor may coast; a separate brake or mechanical restraint needs its own timing and rating | State for which loss of torque has been shown safe       |

: **Stop functions and physical response**: Machine stop categories, related drive functions, and the plant response each leaves to be tested. No stop category alone supplies a safety integrity rating, a brake, galvanic isolation, or a guaranteed stopping distance. {#tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories tbl-colwidths="[18,21,34,27]"}

### Certified safety functions beneath the permission path {#sec-enforcement-certified-functions}

Citing an unrated numerical QP solver or software evidence-age check as the primary hazard control in a safety case fails certification audit immediately, because complex solver code without formal tool qualification and hardware diagnostic coverage cannot carry a safety integrity claim. In an embodied deployment, not all firmware executing the fallback ladder carries formal functional safety certification, so a certification engineer partitions software claims by the integrity of the underlying hardware substrate. On a production machine, formal guarantees rest primarily on a second, lower layer: dedicated safety functions in the motor drives, the optical safety scanner, and the arm's safety controller, each architected and validated to a Performance Level (PL) under ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1]. A Performance Level grades a safety function rather than a component, by the architecture category of its channels, their mean time to dangerous failure, their diagnostic coverage, and their defenses against common-cause failure (@sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning); IEC 61508 grades the same functions by Safety Integrity Level (SIL) [@iec61508]. These hardened functions substantiate the certified protective envelope. Above them, the MCU permission path operates primarily as an unrated performance layer designed to keep the learned policy inside the admissible set, preventing unnecessary trips of the hard safety floor. Only one narrow component of this MCU layer carries a safety rating, the watchdog that revokes authority when the chunk lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-certified-functions
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE ARM'S ROBOT CLASS AND ITS SPEED-AND-SEPARATION DISTANCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the certified-functions table and the arm SSM paragraph below.
# │ Goal:    classify the arm under ISO 10218-1:2025 and evaluate the terms of the
# │          SSM protective separation distance that the chapter already owns.
# │ Show:    arm mass against the Class I limit; S_h, S_r, S_s and their sum;
# │          the human term's share.
# │ How:     RM.arm.mass; EnforcementAuthorityLoss (descending-joint stop);
# │          AISLE.tau_delay as the reaction time if the vision path were the
# │          separation sensor; AISLE.v_human_approach (ISO 13855 K).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementCertifiedFunctions:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    arm_mass = RM.arm.mass  # category: datasheet
    class1_mass = 10.0 * kilogram  # category: standard (ISO 10218-1:2025 Class I limit, per Hartmann et al. 2026)
    class1_speed = 0.25 * meter / second  # category: standard (ISO 10218-1:2025 Class I limit)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 K)
    t_r = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (vision-path delay; not a safety-rated sensing path)
    v_r = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.tcp_speed  # category: illustrative (descending tool point)
    omega = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed  # category: illustrative
    alpha_net = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.alpha_eff  # category: illustrative (bias-reduced)
    s_s = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_eff  # category: illustrative (biased tool stop)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_s = (omega / alpha_net).to(millisecond)
```
