It reserves stopping clearance dynamically, projects candidate controls when a feasible correction exists, and selects a state-matched fallback when communication fails or an invariant breaks. Mathematical safety certificates and algorithmic barrier functions, however, are only as dependable as the underlying real-time compute fabric. Interference through whatever the permission path still shares with the proposers, a board link, a supply rail, a clock, or in some placements a die and a memory bus, can silently consume time that the physical budget already assigned to braking. The final engineering obligation is therefore empirical: verifying that the entire permission pipeline strictly meets its real-time deadlines under worst-case system load on the physical hardware.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-enforcement-history}

The safety certificates developed in this chapter trace their intellectual lineage to classical questions about boundary invariance that predate digital computing. In 1892, Aleksandr Lyapunov demonstrated that one can prove the asymptotic stability of a dynamical system by constructing a scalar, energy-like function, bypassing the intractable problem of solving nonlinear differential equations directly. Mitio Nagumo extended this geometric intuition from isolated equilibrium points to entire sets [@nagumo1942lage]: a closed set traps all future trajectories if and only if the vector field at every point along its boundary points inward or tangent to the boundary surface. Decades later, Aubin formalized this boundary principle for controlled systems within viability theory [@aubin1991viability], characterizing the viability kernel as the set of states from which at least one admissible control input can prevent constraint violations indefinitely. The differential games of @isaacs1965differential introduced an adversarial perspective against worst-case disturbances, which Mitchell, Bayen, and Tomlin later computed on numerical grids through Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis [@mitchell2005time]. Prajna and Jadbabaie translated these boundary arguments into barrier certificates for algebraic system verification [@prajna2004barrier], and Wieland and Allgöwer framed the barrier condition as an affine inequality directly over the control input [@wieland2007constructive]. Ames and collaborators then combined this affine formulation with real-time optimization, creating the control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP) whose solve time can lie in the microsecond range for selected problem sizes and platforms [@ames2014control; @ames2019control]. Contemporary systems engineering treats control barrier functions, reachability analysis, and predictive backup sets as a unified family of safety filters, each continuously monitoring an unverified control proposal against a verified fallback action that remains physically executable [@hsu2024safetyfilter].

The structural pattern that wraps an analytical certificate around a complex model originates in runtime assurance for aerospace and industrial automation. To deploy advanced, unverified control software without risking catastrophic failure, Sha and colleagues designed the Simplex architecture [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using]. Simplex allowed a high-performance experimental controller to drive a live plant while an analytically verified baseline controller and a deterministic switching monitor stood ready to reclaim authority whenever the state neared the edge of the recoverable envelope. Alshiekh and collaborators later transplanted this runtime assurance principle into reinforcement learning under the rubric of shielding [@alshiekh2018safe], using reactive temporal logic specifications to intercept and correct unsafe exploratory actions before they reached the actuators. Physical embodiment, however, introduces contact dynamics that purely kinematic boundary checks cannot govern. Hogan transformed robotic manipulation by introducing impedance control [@hogan1985impedance], which regulates the dynamic relationship (stiffness, damping, and inertia) between environmental forces and manipulator motion instead of tracking brittle position trajectories. Willems provided the rigorous foundation for analyzing such interactions through dissipativity theory [@willems1972dissipative], which formalizes the energy bookkeeping required to guarantee stability across interconnected subsystems. Ferraguti and co-authors embedded that bookkeeping directly into digital software via virtual energy tanks [@ferraguti2013tank]. By tracking energy dissipation within the controller's internal state, energy tanks restrict command authority when stored reserves deplete, preventing explosive instability during abrupt contact or communication latency.

The requirement that a fail-safe mechanism must operate independently of the software it monitors emerged from painful engineering lessons. The Therac-25 accidents recounted earlier in this chapter illustrated the fatal cost of replacing electromechanical safety interlocks with software routines [@leveson1993investigating]; race conditions in unverified code bypassed intended protections and delivered lethal radiation doses to patients. International functional safety standards codified this experience by mandating strict architectural isolation between rated safety functions and the operational systems they supervise [@iec61508; @iso13849part1]. In robotic drivetrains, this separation extends down to hardware-level stop functions, such as safe torque off and safe operating stop, implemented directly within power electronics and drive logic [@iec61800part52]. When runtime enforcement relies on software, temporal predictability becomes just as vital as functional correctness. Worst-case execution-time (WCET) analysis, surveyed comprehensively by Wilhelm and colleagues [@wilhelm2008worst], combines execution models, platform assumptions, and timing evidence to justify latency bounds; empirical observations alone do not establish a certified worst case. The architecture presented in this chapter unites these distinct traditions. A learned policy proposes high-performance actions, an online filter derived from physical stopping budgets preserves forward invariance under its qualified assumptions, and an isolated safety floor supplies its separately qualified protective response. A tamper-evident enforcement log records the exact state evidence that justified each intervention. For further reading, six works trace these ideas from their foundations to current practice:

- @blanchini1999set surveys set invariance in control, tracing the theory from Nagumo's boundary conditions to algorithmic methods for computing polyhedral and ellipsoidal invariant sets, providing the clearest geometric map of the state space that barrier certificates supervise.
- @aubin1991viability develops viability theory, the mathematical framework governing the states from which a constrained system can remain safe indefinitely, and the formal theoretical foundation for the kinetic barriers and viability kernels used throughout this chapter.
- @sha2001using presents the foundational runtime-assurance argument: a complex, unverified controller may retain command authority only while an analytically verified baseline controller, operating within a known recoverable region, stands ready to safely intervene.
- @leveson1993investigating reconstructs the Therac-25 radiation therapy accidents and remains the definitive case study demonstrating why safety interlocks must never depend solely on the software systems they are designed to protect.
- @ames2019control provides a comprehensive tutorial on control barrier functions and quadratic programming safety filters, covering both mathematical underpinnings and physical robotics deployments, and serving as the natural follow-up to @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention.
- @hsu2024safetyfilter unifies control barrier functions, Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, and predictive backup sets into an overarching safety-filter framework, analyzing how learned neural policies can be trained alongside runtime filters to avoid boundary chattering, directly addressing the co-design challenges raised in @sec-enforcement-thesis-bends.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From barrier certificates to SoC placement"}
Can the learned proposers share a chassis, and in some placements a die and a memory bus, with the permission path without delaying it? The enforcement record declares a worst-case cycle inside the permission deadline on every tick. That deadline is a claim about silicon, and a barrier result holds only while the permission path meets it. Every budget in this chapter has assumed the placement Part I adopted as a hypothesis, a discrete safety microcontroller physically separate from the proposers' processor. @Sec-placement puts that hypothesis under load. It partitions the learned proposers and the permission path across compute fabrics and names the loaded tests that would show whether memory starvation, clock throttling, or bus contention can delay permission or fallback, recording them in the placement record.
:::
